Up, down, up and down, 1 Which is the way to London town? Where, where? Up in the air! Close your eyes—and novryou are there! Soon, soon, afternoon, Over the sunset, over the moon, V.. 2 Far, far, over all bar, • , , . Sweeping on from star to star! No, no! low, low, • - Sweeping daisies with my toe, Low, low, to and fro, Slow—slow—slow—slow. ft—William Allingharn in "The Magazine of Art" for May.

IN CANTERBURY CATHEDRAL. 13TH Menai, 1885. " And He buried Igo man knoweth his sepulchre unto this day." Through the dim Minster shrills the march of woe, Over no bier, no mourners following slow "This our dear brother : " God knows where he lies, How he departed; with what obsequies Foul beasts and birds have done the work o' the grave; Or if Nile hides beneath its-kindly wave That broad frank brow and dear uncoffined head, All we know—all we can know—he is dead! And One has buried him: in English hearts Of women, though the passionate anguish darts Through every nerve; of children, crying full fain "I want to be like Gordon ; " and of men, Who, as the worldly scales slip from their eyes, See how a Christian soldier lives and dies. What matter, though his sepulchre unknown, We never find, to mark with needless stone; Nor ever learn who his last word did hear, Who caught his last kind smile, to children dear: God took him. In that hour perchance he saw, Like Moses, all the mystery of the law Of sacrifice—did ha a vision stand Beholding afar off the Promised Land; Order, peace, freedom, purchased by his death, ' And righteousness—the righteousness of faith. Then, organ, peal r Sing, sweet boy-voices clear, "Blessed are the departed!" No, he is here: Not lost, and not "departed : " a great soul Alive through all the ages, sound and whole, Strong, brave, true, tender, humble, undefiled; The lion-heart pure as a little child. Our sons, who read his story without taint, Ceasing to smile, shall own the hero-saint; • And England, rising from her swoon, in pride Shall show how victory came, though Gordon died. —"English Illustrated."—The Author of "John Halifax, Gentleman."

There is but one way to heaven—the way of self- denial, self-sacrifice and unselfish service.—Lyman Abbott. "What is philosophy ?" It is something which en- ables a rich man to say there is no disgrace in being poor. An Americarkeditor offers a reward of five dollars for the best treatise on "How to make outdoor life attrac- tive to the mosquito." God is attracting our regard in and through all things. Every flower is a hint of His beauty; every grain of wheat is a token of His beneficence; every atom of dust is a revelation of His power. Behind the cloud the starlight lurks, Through showers the sunbeams fall; For God who loveth all his works - Hath left his hope with all.— Whittier. Life is warfare, and those who climb up and down steep paths and go through dangerous enterprises are the brave men and the leaders in the camp, but to rest basely at the cost of others' labours is to be a coward, safe because despised.—Seneca. A little four-year-old girl went running into the house the other day, exclaiming: "Mamma, mamma, I've seen Jack Frost! I've seen Jack Frcist !" "Where did you see him, my darling ? " queried the mother. "Oh, I saw the tip of his tail hanging over the eaves." She had seen an icicle. . .

THE BONNY EARL OE MURRAY.—The Earl of Murray, being suspected of participation in the attempt of his cousin Bothwell against the person of King James VI:, fell into disgraae. His arrest was ordered, and the com- mission entrusted to his mortal enemy, the Earl of Huntly. Huntly found the young Earl at Dunnibirsel, the house of his mother, Lady Downe. Murray refusing to surrender, the mansion was fired. The Earl escaped, but was overtaken by his enemies and slain on the 7th of February, 1592. The young Earl of Murray is repre- sented as having been strikingly handsome and accom- Wished, and he was a favourite of the people. The King made a pretence of bringing the Earl of Huntly to trial, in obedience to the popular clamour for revenge; but justice, gave moderation, and the escape of Huntly from gave rise to a report that his Majesty countenanced the murderer out of jealousy for the favour with which the bonny Earl was regarded by the Queen.—" Illustrated British Ballads" for May. PAPER MEN-oF-Watt.—A correspondent of the American Queen gives the following interesting item :—Already there are actnally in existence paper men-of-war of enormous tonnage. A few years ago I was on board the British man-of-war, the "Raleigh," which was cruising in East Indian waters. Pointing to the substantial- looking wooden walls of the vessel, a midshipman asked me one day if I knew what those were made of. I an- swered that probably they were made of teak or oak, and was considerably surprised when he laughed and told aie I was all at sea in more senses than ones "The hull of the ' Raleigh,' " he said, "is really paper hy- draulically pressed. Paper walls in place of the famous wooden walls of England that the poets sing about were adopted by the Admiralty a few years ago as an experi- ment on a few men-of-war. This is one of them that you are now sailing in through the Indian ocean." The paper hull idea, as applied to men-of-war, is a good one, at least in theory. In the old wooden and iron ships the men were more exposed to danger from splinters than direct missiles. Now,paper hulls would at leastdo away with splintering. A shot might hit a vessel and pass right through its side, but the hole would be a clean one, and there would be no splinters until the missile encountered some of the internal machinery and compartments. I do not know whether the English Government has built many of these singular paper boats, but it had one of them at least in the shape of the "Raleigh." In Magazine. 1845 the "American Shorthorn Herd Book" was com- menced, connecting with the Coates series. In 1866 it was estimated that about 800 pure Shorthorns had been brought into the United States and the Canadas ; the seven volumes of the "American Her-Book" then con- tained the pedigrees of 6,400 bulls and over 10,000 females, and its editor estimated the number of pure animals of this breed living in the country at 6,000, one- third males. In 1875 direct importations had reached 1,500, and the pedigreed Shorthorns alive in the United States and Canada were placed at 20,000. The twentieth volume of the "American Shorthorn Herd Book," pub- lished in May, 1881, will carry the number- of recorded bulls to over 40,000, and of cows and heifers to 60,000. Of these, Mr. L. F. Allen, "Herd Book" editor from the first, estimates 93 per cent. as American bred, and that the recorded animals alive in the country number at least 35,000. To these may be added 20,000 well-bred Shorthorns not recorded. The Shorthorns are largely in excess of all other pure bloods in the United States ;and although their influence is felt mainly in the improve- ' ment of beef cattle, many dairymen hold them in high favour, and certain families have made remarkable re- cords at the poll.—Cassella "Dairy Farming" for May. NOTES ON DAIRY Cows.—At a meeting of the Tunbridge Wells Farmers' Club, Mr. Jas. Long, in the course of a lecture on the subject "Is dairy farming worth the atteation of the British agriculturist ?" said if they wished the dairy farmer to make a maximum profit, it , was only fair to assume that the cows should be reared 'on the farm. It was the custom of some to buy their , young stock, and perhaps that was a good plan at the present season of the year, but he looked at it that in forming a dairy herd for profit it was useless to attempt to do business unless they kept the highest class stock,' by which he meant cows that yielded a maximum euan-1 tity of milk, and if they bred for market there was no reason why they should not obtain the highest possible records. He contended that 30 or 40 guineas for a cow was not thrown away when given for the right kind of animal, because they would find no difficulty in selling , I young stock. With regard to the kind of cattle to select, ' he believed the shorthorn possessed more good qualities than any other beast. It whs a good feeder, a deep milker and cheese-maker, much better than any other cow. The practice of some farm labourers was to give food to the cows ad lib., but what he contended was that the scale should be used as much in the question of food as in the question of milk itself, and by trying their cows to see what they yielded, so could farmers obtain a knowledge of what each cow could do en a certain quantity of food. He liked bran for cows because it contained a large proportion of nitrogen, and was bulky, and another food he liked was cocoanut meal. The lat- ter was worthy attention, because it had an agreeable flavour, it went a long way like bran, and it contained a large proportion of fat and oil. One of the most impor- tant items which they looked to in his district was the supply of good water. If a cow was not well watered —and he thought three times a day was necessary for milk—she would fall off to a certainty, therefore it was essential that men who had charge of dairy herds should make a great point of giving the cows pure water.

Councillorehlecxts supported the amendment, as he thought it would be better to test the scheme by one depot before they went to further elpense. Councillor Dixon, in supporting the amendment, said that if he read the papers aright on Saturday it appeared that there was a,nuisance being created at Longford when the material got there, and that nuisance must of necessity be increased if they passed those minutes. They might drive the material to Longford, but when it got there and they commenced to manipulate it there would be a very much greater nuisance. Councillor Surrox said that subject had been already sufficiently ventilated in that Council, and it seemed that those who came there to oppose the proposals that were made came without considering wile her their objections were good or not. (" No, no.") As a proof of this he would point out to them what had been said as to the large price they were paying for the laud, but he said that that land at 3d per yard at 25 years' purchase would be nearly £9OO. That was really the price of the land, and he said further that they could not get land anywhere in that neighbour- hood under 31 per yard as well situated as that for the pur- ogruessixtiopnlo. plots The of lacnodmimn pose. SO they would see they had not fairly considered the itthteeesahmade neighbourhood,had unde r that five was undoubtedly the cheapest. It was quite certain that they would have to do something. Tney would see that the Rural Sanitary Authority bad been having complaints made to them, and therefore if that Council did not think fit to sanction the purchase of that piece of land they should pro- bably be in a worse difficulty than before. In regard to the last piece of land which was offered to them the result of their objection-to the purchase of that piece of land had been a loss to the Corporation of no less than £5OO. 'Councillor FneNcosrn did not object to the buying of that piece of land, but be could not get' it out of his mind that they were acting wrongly in spending at least one- half of that money. He thought the two intercepting de- pots should be allowed to stand over until they proved to the Rural Sanitary Authority that they could cure the nuisance at Longford.

To the Editor of The Examines. Sir,—At last night's Council meeting, I stated that the Sanitary Committee were paying double the market value of the land on the east side of •Lythgoes-lane, proposed to be purchased from W. J. Legb, Esq. This statement was callrd in question, but the following facts will prove that .I did not overstate the case, nor speak without some knowledge of the subject. Less than six months ago, viz' on December lot, 1884, I purchased a plot of freehold land on the east side of Lythgoes-lane, containing 1,488 square yards. This land is within about 100 yards of the plot bought by the Sanitary Committee, is in a better position than theirs, and has good frontage to three streets, viz, Chotley-street, Nor- man-street, and Birehall-street. The vendor received at the rate of nearly 2s 10f 1 per square yard. The Sanittry Committee are paying 13s OD per square yard to W. J. Legh, Esq.. or 7s op if we include the compensation to be paid to Alderman Holmes.—Yours truly, JOHN PLATI'. Lythgoes-lane, Warrington, • May 6th, 1885.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

• The weather has been so favourable to "all kinds of garden operations that all ground work should be in a forward state. Though rain fell heavily on Sunday, the soil at mid-day om Monday worked freely and comfort- ably, and, as on previous days, sowing of seeds and planting could be proceeded with. The showers on Tuesday night helped to settle the soil round the roots of newly-planted subjects, so that as we write every- thing looks fresh and flourishing. Pms.—The earliest sown are now 161 l above ground, and the rows look strong and even: Many, do not sow early, and consequently cannot expect to pick so soon, and if they wish to realise anything for their surplus produce, they, must be content 'With a reduced rate. This is a great oversight, for the seeds of early sowings cost no more than later ones; they occupy only the same space of ground, and altogether they give no more trouble than those that are ready about a fortnight or three weeks later, and the produce is, as a rule, equally good,, but the value little more than one-half of those that first enter the market. If no previous sowing has been made, it should be attended to at once. William the First is a prolific pea for first or second crop, and the flavour is also good. The following are also suit- able :—Advancer, Laxton's Supreme, and Harrison's Glory. In arranging the space for pea rows, it should be borne in mind that the further they are apart the better, and, though this may appear a great waste of land it proves to be real economy. Supposing the rews are five feet distant, nothing can be planted that will grow in such a crowded space, excepting celery, which may be planted just a week or two previous to clearing the peas away. If, however, a distance of Bft. is chosen, we may have a row of celery planted as soon as ready, and on each side, of it colewort cabbage, lettuce, or cauliflowers, without interfering one with the other. BXISTROOT.—This vegetable attains the highest perfec-

tion when grown in a fully exposed situation and a (100 D COMPLEXION moderately rich sandy soil. But it is not so fastidious %X as some Vegetables, and we find it growing in nearly all kind gof soils, but with a fair amount of exposure. The GOOD COMPLEXION Beet is said to contain nearly 12 per cent, of sugar, which ‘3l- varies in proportion to the exposure to sun and air the plants may have been subject to during their season of GOOD COMPLEXION growth. Some varieties are better adapted for certain ‘-'1 soils than others. For poor light soils Cattell's blood-red attains a fair size and quality, whilst on heavy rich soil 41-00 D COMPLEXION it grows too coarse. Dell's black-leaved is naturally " small, and should have liberal treatment to grow it to perfection. Troughton's crimson appears to be inter- GOOD COMPLEXION mediate in size; therefore it should be sown in soil of medium texture. Sowing should be made in drills lkin. ' I-100D COMPLEXION deep and 12in. to 15in. apart, and the plants when tor finally thinned may be 6in. or Bin. distant in the row. I THE FRONT GARDEN.—SOWING SEEDS.—Much injury is GOOD COMPLEXION done to seeds by injudicious sowing. There is an erroneous opinion frequently entertained by persons that are otherwise well-informed that seeds must be well buried in order that the young plants they produce may GOOD COMPLEXION have good hold of the soil, forgetting that as soon as germination takes place the root descends, and the space rtOOD COMPLEXION between its starting point and the surface will be occu- pied by really so much of the stem of the plant, which , at that stage is most delicate, and the less of it that is in (100 D COMPLEXION the soil the better. For the majority of flower seeds we lOr consider a quarter of an inch enough of a covering, and half an inch for the largest kind. All seeds will germi- . (100 D COMPLEXION nate when left alone under favourable conditions if , •-m covered with only their own thickness of soil' but when so near the surface they are exposed to fluctuation, GOOD COMPLEXION which destroys the vitality of all that have weak germi- nating powers. Vermin and birds are also liable to pick up the seeds when so near the surface. There are very GOOD COMPLEXION few, gardens where the soil is in a fine enough condition to sow seeds in that are expected to do well. The quan- tity put over them should be so fine that it would pass GOOD a quarter-inch sieve, and if the ground they are to be sown on is at all lumpy it should be covered with OOD COMPLEXION fine soil, or some of the seeds will drop between the lumps and be an inch or two deep, and the clods will obstruct their upward course. When these little matters , are overlooked we are not surprised that so many are , impressed that they are the recipients of bad seed. I THE WINDOW.—At most of the autumn flower shows IATRIGI;IT'S 004 the Balsam is exhibited by cottagers as a window plant, ' Y V WRIGHT'S COAI but as a rule they are mere phantoms of what they ought to be, and yet they are as easy to grow as any WRIGHT'S COAI Want. They are usually sown thickly in a pot, and vv however many plants may come up they are allowed to WRIGHT'S COAL remain to crowd each other, and are consequently V V spoiled at the commencement. This evil is obviated if AATRIGHT'S COAL only two or three seeds are inserted in a small pot, say Y Y ' three inches diameter, and near the centre in the form wRIGHTS COAL ' of a triangle, and after the plants are Well up reduced to , " 'CU-RIGHT'S COAL one, leaving, of course, the best. In this way the roots v v are not disturbed where the plants require larger pots, wRIGHT'S COAL and growth continues uninterruptedly. The best com- post to sow in is loam and leaf mould in equal parts, WRIGHT'S COAL with one-sixth of sand, and the pots should be filled I within one inch of the top; the remaining space will 1 WRIGHT'S COAL allow for a little top dressing after two of the plants are -WEIGHT'S COAL pulled up. _ V V RIGHT'S CO.

THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. HAMBURGHS. By all who are familiar with domestic poultry it will be conceded that one of the nrost beautiful races of these is that known as Hamburghs, "under which cognomen there are five principal varieties (each of which shall be ' dealt with in proper order), and two or three sub- varieties. These all have the same distinctive features, namely, large rose comb; smallish, closely sot bodies, well f urnished tails, the cocks with long sickles, and fine, clean legs; but it cannot be claimed that they were all originally of the salve fpñly, HOW they derived the • • hanie is not certainly known. Upon 4ila - point, in a work published more than 30 years ago, the writer says : " Why it should be called the Hamburgh fowl seems in- explicable, except upon the supposition that the Levant merchants residing at Hamburgh introduced them from Turkey or elsewhere, and that from Hamburgh they were exported into this country. By a similar transit did our Black Hamburgh grapes derive their names, for they are certainly natives of Spain, imported by the Hamburgh merchants, and first known to us as Ham- burgh grapes, because purchased there. Whatever may haye been its place of origin, or however its present name may have been derived, it would appear that the Hamburgh fowl was among the occupants of the poultry yard of our monasteries as early as the beginning of the fourteenth century, since Chaucer has described a cock in their possession, which was evidently of the Golden Hamburgh breed." Mr. Tegetmeier, in his poultry book dealing with tins points, says :—" There is no doubt that these fowls had originaliy no title whatever to the name of Hamburghs, which was in the first instance given to them by some gentleman connected with the early Birmingham shows. It is true that the pencilled birds formerly were, and still are, imported in consider.ible numbers from Hol- land, under the name of Pencilled Dutch and Dutch Every-day Layers, but the spangled birds appear to be ex-Ausively English fowls, and are essentially distinct varieties, differing in size, plumage, and in the formation of the skull; and lastly, the name of llamburgh had previously been applied to one of the varieties of feather- crested fowl, now with an -equal absence of geographical correctness known as Polish:' As a confirmation of this last statement, we may add that in an old work (Miner's) in the writer's possession, the illustration given as " Spangled Hamburghs," undoubtedly represents Polish. There are the large crest, the shape, and the plumage of the Polish, without any resemblance what- ever to the Hamburgh varieties as now known. To come to a later authority, we find in Wright's "Book of Poultry" the following There is very little doubt that the two varieties known as Pencilled Ham- burghs were really imported from Holland, having been, for years previously to the present name, well known under the title of Dutch Every-day Layers or Everlast- ing Layers, and having been largely imported both at a comparative recent date, and on many former occasions of which there is historial evidence. The spangled and black varities, on the contrary, are as evidently a native English breed of considerable antiquity, having been kept and shown at village exhibitions beyond the memory of man; and the spangled breeds, besides the difference in marking, presenting differences of shape, being larger, plumper, and samewhat coarser 'in make, besides a greater width across the skull. These latter varieties were always known under the name of the Lancashire Mooneys, and Yorkshire Pheasant fowls, while the blacks were called Black Pheasant fowls, until almost immediately after the establishment of the Great Birmingham Show the authorities there—chiefly, we be- lieve, owing to the influence of the Rev. E. S. Dixon— grouped all under the general name of Ilamburghs, and the paramount authority of that great gathering was sufficient to make the new nomenclature:general." Thus much for the historical part of this naming. Whether the word Hamburgh is the best name that could have been selected to designate the varieties grouped under it is doubtful. Unfortunately, like in the case of the Polish, it gives a sense of locality which is mislead- ing, and, unless for the reason in the first quotation given above, it is difficult to see why it should have been selected. But there are so many things in life we cannot understand, and the fact of the name Hamburgh being a generally accepted term makes all objections to it frivolous. That it is a decided advantage to have all these varieties included in one section is undoubted. No one can compare them without seeing that the same type and characteristics run through all. In general contour they are the same; the shape of head.and comb are the same in all; the tails show the same fulness, with sweep- ing sickles; all the varieties are prolific layers and non- sitters, and are of the active nature which makes it so difficult to keep them within bounds. Therefore, the benefit from the classification is undoubted. As layers they are perhaps the best of all domestic fowls, and 220 eggs per annum is no uncommon average for a single hen. But the eggs are rather small for market purposes, and this, of course, militates against their adoption upon farms. When used for crossing with a larger breed they are .very valuable indeed, and we have often recom- mended them.

All the Hamburgh races have the characteristic of beauty. This, with their graceful forms, has made them popular as fancy fowls. The rich colour' regular spangling or pencilling, and, in case of the blacks, the beetle-green plumage; the neat, shapely head, the long tail, all combine to exalt it into one of the handsomest breeds of poultry. There are some other varieties, or offshoots, than those mentioned, chief amongst which is the red cap. This is very popular in some parts of Derbyshire. It is much larger and coarser than the Hamburgh, but is valued for its great laying powers. SEASONABLE kiINTS.

Chickens require special attention at this time of the year, and the breeder must see that all their wants are attended to, and that they are regularly fed and housed in a comfortable manner, but yet have plenty of air. The weather has lien very warm of late, and more fresh air is needed. Too much cannot be given, so long as the birds are not exposed to draughts, and it is as dangerous for fowls as human beings to breathe vitiated air. If there are trees about, and the older chicks prefer to roost in them, they may be allowed to do so, as it will make them hardier and stronger.

As to the third paragraph, it referred to a district of which there ex'eted no legal, historical, or conventional definition. Therefore he maintained that there was no froatier of a definite charac- ter with regard to which one Power could bring another Power to account and exact of it the performance of a cer- tain engagement. If, with the transactions of such diffi- culty and anxiety in hand, the Government could not be trusted with this authority under the responsibility of the future judgment of Parliament, the sooner the House released them from all responsibility the better. He had not the smallest objection to meet a propose! to so release them. He had met it before. In fact, during the present Parliement the question had been raised about as often as it had in a the other eleven Parliame,bta with which he had been connected put together. But let that question be raised with knowledge, and not under circumstances which would seriously injure national and imperial interests. (Cheers.) Mr. CHAPLIN urged the Government to consent to a post- ponement of the vote, and moved the adjournment of the debate. _ .

Mr. GLADSTONE warmly opposed the motion on the ground that it would create an impression abroad that Ear'lament was wavering; but Sir S. Nonrucont thought this an en- tirely baseless apprehension, and remarked that if any un- certainty existed it was because of the difficulty which had been found in obtaining a clear understanding of what the Government was doing. Lord HARTINGTON asked whether the Opposition meant to refuse to vote the supplies until they had discussed the policy of the Government. Such a course would be most in- convenient to the public service.—Sir B. Cross and Mr. O'Donnell supported the adjournment; but on a division'the motion was negatived by 18t to 114. A motion for the adjournment of the House was moved by Baron DE WORAD?, and Sir M. HICKS- BEACH again ap- pealed to the Government to afford the House another op- portunity to discuss the subject; but Mr. GLADSTONE re- peated that injury would result from hesitation by the House to grant the vote, and said he could not and would not depart from the decision he had arrived at. .

Sir S. NORTHCOTH joined in the appeal to the Government to consent to the adjournment, and Lord R. CHURCHILL quoted from a speech at Lord Hartington on the Vote of Credit of 1878 in favour of an adjonrnment.—The motion was negatived by 169 to 111. Mr. S. HERBERT then moved the adjournment of the de- bate, which after an animtted discussion was negatived by 164 to 106.

Mr. BRODIE moved the adjournment of the llouse Mr. Guinsrom said if the Opposition would give the Government the Vote of Credit, a discussion could take place afterwards. sty on the Censolidated Bill, on Thursday, or on going into Committee. Sir S. NORTITCOTB agreed to this course. The motion for adjournment was neg,tivsd without a division' but the Irish Party challenged a divisicn on the Vote of Credit— For the vote l3O Against 2o— 110 The Submarine Cables Bill passed through Committee. The Trustees Relief Bill was read a second time. The House adjourned at 240. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. • •

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at 4-30. Tun PROPOSED ARBITRATION.—EarI De LA WARE: I wish ta ask, as to the uropostl of the Government with re- gard to the Afghan frontier question, whether i, is_to be understood as one of mediation or arbitration P That is to say, an, we Inviting the good offices of a friendly Power, or are we placing the question at issue in the hands of an irrPriponsible umpire whose decision would be final P—Earl GRANVILLF, : There are one or two peers on the other side of the House who have not as strong a conviction as I have that nobody is capable of putting a question in a cicarer way than the noble lord on the front Opposition Bench. Ido not think it necessary when he has put a question that one of his noble friends should come to the rescue with another question on the following day to make it clear. At the same time, I must say that I have nothing to aid to the answer I gave yesterday. As there is in the question of the noble Earl something in the nature of cen- sure upon what has been done, I should like to sty that what has been done appears to use a very sensible and honourable proceeding on the part of the statesmen con- cerned. In private life I can conceive nothing better calcu- lated to promote a good understanding than when a matter of practical great importance is under discussion, and a disagree- able and regrettable incident occurs, which to a certain degree affects the honour of the individuals concerned, and which may be open to counter statement and contention, to refer that extraneous question to the judgment of some friend in whom they have perfect confidence to enable the matter to be closed with honour to both sides. That appears to me to be exactly what occurred in this case. The two nations were discussing a question of great importance, namely, the delimitation of the frontier of Afghanistan, and the regrett- able incident occurs which, rieditly or wrongly, seems to affect their honour. Instead of going to the ultima ratio, I think it was an honourable proceeding on our part to pro- pose that reference should be made to the judgment of the head of some friendly State, and I think it was equally creditable and honourable to Russia that she Mould have accepted thtt proposal. (Hear, bear). RAILWAY BRAKES.—EarI DE LA WARE inquired whether it was intended to take any steps to make it compulsory upon railway companies to adopt the recommendations of the Board of Trade in regard to the adoption of efficient brakes —Lord SUDELEY said the Government did not in- tend to propose any legislation this session with regard to railways.

CREMATION —ln reply to Lord Onslow, the Earl of DAL- HOUSIE said her Majesty's Government did not consider it any part of their duty either to encourage or discourage the practice of cremation. They had no power of dealing with the matter.
Their lordships rose at 450. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIIESDAY. '

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN.—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Mr. ilawaay, said instructions had been sent to Lord Wolseley, in accordance with the statement recently made, that it was not intended to prosecute the war in the Soudan, and corn- municttions were passing between Lord Wolseley and the War Office with the object of carrying those instructions into effect. Tun AFGHAN CRISIS.—TIie PREMIER informed Sir Henry Wolff that in consequence of the decision that negotiations in regard to the main points connected with the delimitation of the Afghan frontier should be carried on in London, Sir Peter Lumsden and Colonel Stewart have bees instructed to return hems to give their assistance in the matter. In reply to Mr. Puleston, the Premier said that by command of her Mijesty the Queen there bed been conveyed to the na- tive princes and chiefs in India who had recently displayed conspicuous loyalty an expression of the warm feeling her Majesty entertained on the subject. In some cmversetion on the business of the week, Mr. Gladstone intimated that be could not promise any papers relating to Afghan affairs by Thursday.—Sir M. H. BEACH suggested that the debate should be postponed till Menlay.—Mr. GLADSTONE offered no objection.—The matter was not, however, finally de- cided, being left over for further consideration.—A series of questions of a controversial character were addressed to the Premisr by Lord Randolph Churchill, Mr. Asbmead Bartlett, Mr. Onelow, and other members of the Opposition, but they did not succeed in eliciting any further informa- tion.

THE ENGLISH REGISTRATION BILL.—On the motion to go into Committee on the English Registration Bill, Sir MASSEY Lop s moved an amendment declaring that the House, while desirous of facilitating in every way the registration of voters, is of opinion that, inasmuch as the preparation of the register for Parliamentary elections is a matter of national rather than local concern, the expenses connected therewith should not be imposed on ratepayers in counties and boroughs, and levied in respect of the oc- cupation of a single description of property. The bon. baronet, at whose rising the crowded House instantly emptied, protested against imposing farther burdens on pro- perty, and urged in amplification of his amendment that the charges of registration being for the national benefit should be charged on the Imperial funds.—The amendment was seconded by Mr. PELL.—Mr. HENRY Forman, dealing as far as was possible under the peculiar circumstances of the debate with the general question of local taxation' de- livered an able speech. which attracted and maintained the flagging attention of the House. He urged that the pro- posal of the Government tow trds meeting objections from the other side was fair and adequate. The Under Secretary, on resuming his seat, received the warm congratulations of the Premier on his maiden speech as a Minister —Sir Walter Barttelot, Mr. Sampson Lloyd, and Mr. R. Paget supported the amendment before an audience which had again fallen to the point of zero.—Mr. W. Fowler, Mr. Heneage, and Mr. Cropper supported the proposal of the Government.—The discussion was con- tinued by Sir R. Cross, Mr. Illingworth, Mr. Holdsworth, Mr. Duckham, Mr. Whitley, Mr. Harris. Mr. Round, Mr. Arnold, Mr. Ecroyd, Mr. S. Leighton, Mr. Ackert, and Mr. P. W. Mutt z.—At this stage the debate, always threatening collapse, seemed to have reached its ultimate point, and the Speaker had risen to put the question, when Sir M. H. Mach interposed, and made a epe ch in support of Sir Massey Lopes' amendment—Sir Charles Dike wound up the debate on the part of the Government, Mr. Sclater- Booth somewhat unexpectedly continuing the discussion.— Mr. Warton, 'sneaking amid a storm of cries of "divide, under which he finally succumbed, attempted to lengthen the proceedings.—At half-past twelve the division took place, the amendment being rejected by 240 votes against 237, a narrow majority much cheered by the Conservatives. Tile House then went into Committee on the Bill.—Pro- gress was reported, and the House was counted out at 25 minutes past one. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESPAY. The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes past twelve o'clock.

REGISTRATION OF VOTERS.—The House went into com- mittee on the Registration (Occupation Voters) Bill, re- suming at clause 4 —Mr. ARNOLD proposed that a revision court should be held in each division of a divided borough where such an arrangement should appear to be expedient for the convenience of voters.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL opposed, and the amendment was rejected by 77 to 44. An amendtront was proposed by Mr. MABust to confer on gradu- ates of Oxford and Cambridge the same residential as well as University franchise which is enjoyed by the Students of Trinity College, Dublin.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL declined to ACC pt the amendment, on the ground that it was an attempt to bring about an extension of the franchise in a Registration Bill.—Professor Stuart having put in a plea

for the enfranchisement of the body to which he belonged at the University, Mr. }UmEs remarked upon the incrin- sicency of the law which, whilet allowing Mr. Stu err to occupy a seat in Pa-liamenr, would not permit him to vote for the borough of Cambridge, in which he resided.—Upon the question being put, the amendment WAS agreed to with. out a division. A new clause was proposal by Mr. H. DAVEY, that medical relief should not be deemed to constitute paro- chial relief within the meaning of the Representation of the People Acts.—lt was opposed by the ATTORNEY GENERAL on the grouad that it would be an inducement to people to give up their independence and to pauperise themselves.— Mr. J. COLLINGS argued that in the rural districts if a man were disfranchised on account of medical relief it would really be disfranchising him on account of his poverty.— The proposal was negatived by 170 to 102.—Sir M. LOPES gave notice that in coast (pence of the very strong expres- sion of opinion which had neen given during Tuesday night's discussion he shall move to recommit the bill on report. BURIAL BOIRDS.—The Burial Beards Contested Elections Bill was read a third time. The House adjourned at 5-55. HOUSE OF LORDS—THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock.

THE REVOLT IN CANADA.—The Earl of DERBY, having read telegrams receivtd from Canada relating to the engage- merts on Sunday between the Colonial troops and the in- surgents, was asked by the Earl of Redesdale what the Indians were contending for, and whether they deserved relief.—The COLONIAL SECRETARY replied that he was not in a position to give any author.tative information, and he believed that the Canadian Government themselves were very much in the same perplexity as Lord Redesdale as to the real causes of the outbreak. FRIENDLY SocinTint,.—Earl GREVILLE moved the second reading of a bill proposing to deal with the growing evil of the insolvency of Friendly Societies by making the certifi- cate of an actuary an ab,olute condition of registration.— Lord InuaLow, on the part of the Government, declined to accept the measure, as it was a retrograde step. and would tend to create a false sense of security. The bill was thrown out by a majority of one, there being 33 "net con- tents" against 32 contents." .

ENGLAND AND CirtativlLLE made a short statement on the hopes of peace in reply to a question put by Lord Stratheden and Campbell on the regulation for the admission of foreign ships to the Dardanelles.—The FOREIGN SECRETARY remarked that he did not believe that war with Russia was perfectly unavoidable, nor did he agree that if war came we should wage it with every possible dis• advantage against us and with every possible advantage in favour of Russia. Their Lords4iias adjourned at five minutes to six o'clock. 110U,E OF COMMONS.—TRUIISDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o:clock. LaNcastrtnE BILL.—The Southport and Cheshire Lines Extensioo Railway Bill and the S!aly bridge Gas Transfer Bill were read a third time.

Later in the evening, the Prime Minister stated that Sir P. Lumeden's cominision was still in force, but as the negotiations were to be carried on in London and only details would be examined on the spot, it had not been considered proper employment for an officer in the position of Sir P. Lumsden, and that was the reason why he had been instructed to repair to this coun- try. The right hon. gentlemen added that there was no in- tention of postponing the settlement of the main points of the frontier till the arrival of Sir P. Lumsden. SUPPLY. —The rest of the evening was devoted to the Baltic to the north-west. By her conquest of the Orenburg country, Russia was enabled to cross the Ural the consideration of the Army Estimates in Committee of Mountains, and open up additional communications with Supply. ' her previously-acquired Siberian possessions. Intent upon increasing the foothold already secured in Asia, small aggressions were gradually and almost imper- ceptibly made until, in 1725, a strike was made towards the south, and another large slice of Siberia—bounded by Omsk on the extreme north- east, Kabana on the north-west, and thence run- ning almost in a direct line, as shown in the map, as far as Lake Balka.sh, and from there formed a junction with the river Tchu, thus securing possession of addi- tional territory in the neighbourhood of Eastern Tur- kestan. Having now obtained a long and well-defined frontier on the north and east, it was determined to move backward to the west, and attack the people inhabiting the wide stretch of country lying between Lake Balkash on the east and the Caspian See to the west. The idea was successfully accomplished by 1796, and the Russian Empire at once became vastly increased and consolidated. This move showed Russia's policy of not having a large empire consisting of isolated patches I far apart from each other, but of keeping all her newly acquired possessions well in hand anecompact. The following year-1797--the Czar, Paul 1., struck west of the Caspian, and claimed and kept Berl:lend, just beyond the northern frontier of Persia. Here a position was secured, which in time enabled Russia to enter the Shah's territory, which she did in 1802, when the pro- vince of Georgia was ceded to her demands. Persia smarted under the loss of a province she had attained by conquest, and burned for revenge. Ultimately, at the instigation of France, war was commenced withl Russia, and after two years of conflicts disastrous to the Persians, the Treaty of Gulistan was signed in 1813, by which Persia gave to Russia all her possessions to the north of Armenia, and the right of navigation in the Caspian Sea. After further reducing the Persian power in Western Asia, and after a deadly struggle for 32 years, subduing the Caucasian mountaineers, who occupied the country between the Caspian and Black Seas, and by which closer communications with the Crimea was rendered possible. Russia further encroached on Persia in Central Asia in 1856. Since that time all Russia's efforts have apparently been to draw nearer and nearer to Afghanistan. In 1860 the whole of the valley of the Amur was annexed by General Kauf- mann, one of the results of this being that in 1865 the north-east portion of Turkestan. with Tashkent, followed in the same direction. Through Kaufmann's exertions in 1878 Samarcand and a large tract of adjoining terri- tory was ceded to Russia. On June 10th, 1873, the same general captured Khiva. In consequence, however, of a treaty between England and Russia, the victorious troops were withdrawn, but the campaign greatly extended Russian dominion, and established the unconditional authority of the Czar in Central Asia. The last act of General Kaufmann was the invasion of Khohan in 1875. This place is a mountainous region about 300 miles north of the Hindoo Koosh, which is on the borders of 4orthern India, and the north-east of Afghanistan. There is very little danger, however, of attack on India irom this point, as the natural obstacles to be overcome may be considered insurmountable. Russia's present point of attack is from the western side of Afghan, a few hundred miles from Herat.

_ WE S LEYANI9I AT WAR RIN GTON. The anniversary services in connection with the Silver. street (Wesleyan) Sunday school were held in Wesley Chapel, Bewsey-read, when the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. F. C. Balms (Barnsley), an address to the scholars and friends being given in the afternoon by the Rev. G. E. Cutting. The collection for the day amounted to £33 15s 10d. On Monday evening the annual meeting and social aatheriog was held in the same building, when there was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by the Rev. J. McTurk, who was supported by the Revs. G. E. Haime, J. H. Jones, and G. E. Cutting, and other gentlemen.—The Secretary (Mr. R Silcock) announced the receipt of a tele- gram apologising for the absence of the Rev. E. L. Jones, ' and proceeded to read the annual report. The. committee of Silver-street Sunday school had pleasure in stating that its condition and prospects continued satisfactory. The num- bers on the books were: Teachers and officers 38, average attendance: morning 11, afternoon 24; members of society 26 ; scholars 461; average attendance, morning 95, afternoon , 310. The Band of Hope new numbered about 150 members. Weekly meetings were held during the season for members only, and nine public meetings had been held during tbe present season. The committee felt sanguine in saving that this branch of the work compared favourably with others. One of the members of the Band of Hope, Master , William Arthur Stone, who was about 14 years of age had dietinguished himself in a competitive examination held in connection with the United Kingdom Band of Hope Union. A prize had been secured by him out of 3 000 competitors, and he had also secured one from Silver-street and one from the Warrington Band of Hope Union. Silver-street Band of Hope was the only one in Warrington that had gained a prize. These, the committee thought, were gratifying results, that incited the workers to further diligence. During the last eight weeks chil- dretee mission services had been held on Sunday evening, and had been well attended by the ragged and outcast chil- dren of the locality. In the library they had 305 volumes, with 40 readers. Financially the school was in good con- dition, being carded on economically and satisfactorily. The receipts for the past year, including balance in hand, amounted to £54 5s 3d, and the expendi.ure left a balance in hand of £4 us 9d. After referring with regret to the loss of several teachers, the report proceeded to speak of the or- ganisation of a brass band, a movement which had been ex- ceedingly well met. The sun, of nearly £56 had been re- ceived towards the fund being raised in connection with this matter, and there now remained a balance of about £2O to be made up.—The choir then sang a solo and chorus from the Messiah, Mr. Reddish taking the solo in a highly credi- table manner.—Mr. Bowden, in a short address, said that he knew of no institution in Warrington that had accomplished a greater work than that effected by the Silver-street Sun- day School—effected, too, under great difficulties. (Ap- plauee.)—The Rev. J. H. Jones referred to the important work done by the select classes, which, he said, were becom- ing a link between the Sunday school and the church. In our Sunday schools there was a vast home tnissionary agency, which had never been utilised as it should leo, for Sunday school teachers had an influence over the parents of their scholars, not possessed by other workers.—Addresses were also delivered by the Rev. G. E. Cutting and the Rev. F. C. Haime, choruses were given by the choir with solos sung by Miss Horton and Mr. Dell, and after the meeting had been brought to a conclusion refreshments were par- taken of in the large vestry.

ALLEGED MURDER AT SOUTH SHIELDS —About eighteen months ago the dead body of Hobert Hudson, a watchman, was found on board a steamer lying idle at South Shields, and it was clear from the position of the body that he could not have been accidentally killed. The mystery was not in any degree cleared until within the past few days, when the police arrested a man, named iqq.iarry, and a woman, Catherine Connerton, on suspicion of murdering the watch- man. The male rrisoner is add to have made a statement that he and Connerton went on board the vessel to rob Hud- son, who was knocked down the hold and killed. They rifl,d his pockets, and then dragged the bo ly to the place, beneath the boilers, where it was found. The prisoners are under remand.

SODDEN DEATH OF THE EARL OF DUDLEY.—The Earl of Dudley died very suddenly early on Thursday from con- gestion of the lungs, at his London residence, Dudley House, Dark-lane, at the age of 67. His lordship hid been iII or,lv two days. He is succeeded by William Humble Viscount Ednam, who was bore in MaY.,1867. THE AFGHAN CRISIS.
PEACE PROSPECTS -RUSSIAN SUB- MISSION TO ARBITRATION ON
THE PENJDEH INCIDENT.

Sy. PEritaSßnitrt, Sur/guar.—After a very anxious and troubled week a sudden calm has fallen upon us. lam in a position to give you an exact narrative of the events. On the 25th ult. M. de Stall received two notes from Lord Granville one explainiag the reasons why the Penjdeh in- cident still seemed to her Majesty's Government to call far explanation, the other formally proposing to submit to ar- bitration the question of the alleged infraction of the agree- ment concluded on the 17th of March. The gist of these notes was telegraphed by the Russian Ambassador to his Government, and very soon spread abroad in St. Petersburg. Opinions varied as to whether the new English proposals would be accepted or not. The press, having an inkling cf the matter, spoke decidedly against arbitration, but nothing , could be known for certain until M. de Giers had found an I opportunity of communicating with the Emperor. This occurred on Tuesday, when the Foreign Minister went to Gatschina, and his return was awaited with extraordinary anxiety, for it was felt that England had said her last word, and that the rejection of these proposals meant war. An evening party which was held at the German Embassy that night promises to become as historical as the Duchess of Richmond's ball at Brussels on the eve of Waterloo. Their Imperial Majesties were not present, but nearly all the Grand Dukes and Duchesses were, and a b:illiant as- semblage, besides diplomatists and Russian magnates. Peace er war was the question on everyone's lips. Peace or war was the one subject of conversation, and the faces of all who were likely to know more than their neighbours were eagerly scanned for some sign of the results of M. de Glare's journey. The Foreign Minister, of course, attracted most attention, more especially when he was engaged in a long and earnest conversation with Sir E. Thornton. It trans- pired in the course of the evening that it had been decided to submit the English proposals to a council composed of a committee of Ministers, and the mere fact that the pro- posals had net been thought acceptable outright gave rise to the most melancholy prognostications. On Wednesday ac- cordingly exchange fell almost as low as it did after the first battle of P learns, and the anxiety grew intense. This feel- ing was increased by the telegraphic summary of Mr. Glad- stone's speech, and by rumours of an Imperial journey to Moscow to launch a proclamation of war. Ihe text of Lord Granville's Note was impatiently expected, but it only reached St. Petersburg on Thursday evening, and on Friday it was the subject of deliberation at Gatscbina' where a Council assembled, consisting of the Emperor, M. de Giers, the Grand Dukes Vladimir and Alexis, M. Vanofsky, Min- ister of War ; Admiral Shestakoff, Minister of Marine ; M. de Leanoff, Minister of Public Instruction • M. Buntne, Finance Minister ; MM. Wrontzoff and Daekoff, of the Household; and M. Pobedonostsheff, Procureur of the Rely Synod. Meantime M. de Giers had obtained from the Eaglieh Government some slight modification in the terms proposisz arbitration, el as to make the proposal a little more palatable, and tne result was that though still not ac- voted out of hand, the proposal was virtually agreed to.— Standard.

.. _ The Daily 3eias save :—No message was received from St. Petersburgh yesterday (Monday). lite communication received on Saturday afternoon, which, as Mr. Gladstone's statement showed, confirmed in detail the announcement in the Daily News of Saturday morning, is regarded by her Majesty's Government as a full and final ac- ceptance by Russia of the proposals made in Lord Gran- villa's despatch. TBIPUL, THURSDAY (via Meshed Sarrday).—The dam at Ktrahand, 70 miles north of Sarakhs, hoe burst. Great damage has been done to the surrounding district, the coun- try being flooded for miles round. The Russians are mak- ing strenous efforts to repair the breach. CALCUTTA, MONDAY.—It is stated that the Indian Govern- ment, besides the 10,000 Snidars already presented, is send- ing he Ameer 10,000 Martini-Ilenris, 10,000 Enfield. 130,C00,000 rounds of amunition, 27 Nordenfeldts, and a large quantity of accoutrements.—Times. COPENIIIOEN, TUESD A pacific solution of the Angloallussian difficulty is here regarded as certain. No doubt is enterttined that Vie King of Denmtrk will act as arbitrator, and the fullest confluence is expressed. in his judgment. THE RECALL OF SIR P. LUMSDEN. Sir P. Luinsden has been recalled solely for the purpose of assisting the Government with his advice upon the nego- tiations that are about to take place in London for toe delimitation of the Russo-Afghan frontier. Pending his arrival negot ations will go on, bet nothing &finite as regards the more important points of delimitation under discussion will be concluded. At present it is the intention of the Government that Sir I'. Lumsden should personally superintend the final marking out of the boundary which he may advise the Government to adopt. SIMLA, WEDNEtaiv.—The Atneer arrived at Cabal on April 30. Sir l'eter Lumsden is stated to have resigned owing to disagreement with the policy of the home Govern- ment.

The Daily News says that Sir Peter Lumsden is expected La artive in London in the first week in June. Major Ridgeway, an officer attached from the first to Sir Peter Lnmsden's Commission, and having intimate know- led;, e of the frontier question, is now in charge of the camp at lirpul, and will remain to complete the work of delitnita• lion on the spot as soon as the male points shall have been settled in London. Major Ridgeway has the assistance of four other Engineer officers.

div.head: ENGLISH WAR PREPARATIONS.
div.p: ENGLISH WAR PREPARATIONS.

On Saturdoy afternoon the Liverpool steamers which have been engaged by the Government as armed cruisers, were officially inspected in the Liverpool docks. Perfect satisfaction was expressed with the way in which all the vessels were being prepared for sea. The National Steam Co's. steamer France has I)een chartered for the conveyance of cavalry. A new 80-ton gun has been successfully moun- ted on the Inflexible. It is stated that Rear Admiral Sir A. Hoskiss will be ' given the command of a fleet formed of the following ships,

t ,getter with others vet to be Eelected, for acr iise prebe ext,iiding into the Baltic —H .r Majastv's ships Re- nulse, 11 reales, BePeisle, Shannon, Penelope, Lord %Verdi n, Valiant, Hector, and Defence. The transport Kimberley commerced to fill up with stores on Monday. She will take 4,000 tons of co .l to the Car,', and convoy at least one of the gunboats boned for that station. At Portsmouth Dockyard on Saturtiaav no fewer than 150 peneiorers had rejoined the navy as gunners. Considerable difficulty is experienced in finding sufficient engineers for ships to be cemmissiened, and engineer s:udeets are there-. fore being appointed as acting assiktuits. A strong detach- ment of Marine Artillery are ordered to leave Eastney Bar- racks, Portsmouth. for the China station, for service in war ships. Men on leave have le:en re-called to join the Mar- ine Artillery. Patterns of the various stores iequired by the Government, and for the supply of which tenders have been invited, are on view at Woolwich. In the commiseariet warehouses at Woolwich there is a reserve of food equal to three million days' ration?, and nearly four hundred men are continually employed in receiving and packing new stock. Monday being the date fixed for the assembly for per- manent service of the men of the 16 regiments of the First Class Army Reserve, considerable animation and activity prevailed at the depots of the respective regiments. Within 24 hours from the issue of the notication a considerable number had joined, and each day since has witnessed rich large accessions to the strength as to lead to the impression that tbe absentees,when Monday's roll was called, were very small. The Northern District furnishes the largest number of mee. At the depot of one regiment of the line ordered to to furnish 300 non-commissioned officers and men, 681 absentees amounted to only half a dozen. The number of men in this district due on Tuesday was 19 sergeants, 25 corporals and 1,308 men for the West Yorkshire Regiment, BorCer Regiment, North Lancashire Regiment, Durham Light Infantry, •Northumberland Fusilliers, Liverpool Regiment, Warwickshire Regiment, and East Lancashire Regiment, the depots at which they reepectively join being York, Carlisle, Preston, Newcastle, Warrington, Warwick, and Burnley. All the above will at the earliest possible moment, after they are medically examined and equipped, embark for India to join the battalions in General Sir D. M. Stewart's command. Wives and families of the men who sign for permanent service will not accompinv the man, but will be granted separate allowances at the rate of BJ. a day for the wife and 2d a day for each girl under 16 or boy under 14 years of age. It is stated that a Kentish commander of Volunteers has received private intimation that it is not improbable the Government will cause it to be signified :te the Voluut,er force that the service of such of its members as may be wil- ling to be embodied for a period will be accepted. The New York Teibune published a telegram from Aspin- wall reefing that the Chilian war-vessel Esmeralda, now at Panama, will be turned over to England in case of war, in order to fight the Russian gunboat Djiggit, which is at present kovering near Panama. The activity with which war preparations are centinucd is illustrated by an announcement publiehed by the Paris National. It is to the effect that the well-known firm of Hotchkiss, the manufacturers of revolver canon, received on Monday an order for 20047-millimetre guns for the British Government. At two pen. Russia sent in an order for 100 37-millimetre guns ; and an hour later Messrs. Hotchkiss received an order for 50 guns of the same kind from the Italian Government.

Orders were given on Wednesday to all responsible offi- cials concerned in the special preparations to in no way re- lax their efforts in completing the equipment of the ships contracted for as cruisers, transports, and gunboats. The hiring by the Admiralty of the following tug boats and small steam vessels to be armed as gunboats was finally concluded on Wednesday : Flying Kestral, 133 tons; Fly- ing Hurricane, 154 ; Dauntless, 120; Africa,.l22 ; Recovery, 532; Gipsy, 115; Scythian, 240; Dynamic, 854; Gal. vanic, 709 and Weatherall. These are now being pre- pared at different arsenals for receiving their armaments. SYDIQEY, WEDNESDAY —The Hon. W. B. Dailey, Acting Colonial Eecretary for New South Wales. has addressed a circular telegraphic despatch to-day to the .premiers of all Australian colonies, suggesting a united indemnification against all the losses inflicted upon persons refusing sup- plies er oral to the enemy's cruisers, such indemnity to be guaranteed by all the colonies. The memorandum has been based upon the proposals made in an able paper drawn up by Rear-Admiral Tryon, commander-in-chief on the Austra- lian station.

div.head: RUSSIAN PREPARATIONS.
div.p: RUSSIAN PREPARATIONS.

Sr. PETERSBURG, WEDNESDRY.-A telegram from Khab- arovka, aated the 23rd Aprii, announces that on that day Adjutant-General Baron Koiff Governor-General and Com- mander-in-Chief of the Amur territory. left for Vladivos- took by steamer on the Amur river, wLich was then becom- ing free of ice. An imperial order has been issued. according to which the First Railway Battalion of Reserve will in future bear the designation of the First Transcaspian Railway Battalion. A second Transcaspian Railway Bat- talion is also to be formed.
THE KING OF DENMARK AS • ARBITRATOR.

L.OPENITAGEN, WEDNESDAY, 10 - yesterday's Council of State the King finally announced his intention of accepting the office of arbitrator between England and Russia, if requested to act in that capacity by both parties. His Royal Highness expressed his belief that the only ques- tion to be referred to hien would be whether there had been any infringement of the arrangement arrived at by England and Russia on the 17th of March. In this capital there is a very general feeling of satisfaction at the prospects of a settlement. Some of the extraordinary defenca measures which were ordered to maintain the integrity of Denmark when an Anglo-Russian conflict seemed certain have now been deferred, and will propably be abandoned.

It is rumoured in official circles that General Zebenoy will be ordered either to St Petersburg or to assist in the negotiations about to take place upon the delimitation of the Russo• Afghan frontier. No official notification has been made to that effect, but the RIVBI tn General's presence in this country, along with Sir Peter Lumsden, would be viewed with satisfaction.

THE OCCUPATION OF PENJDEH. TEHERAN, THIIRSDAY.—In tel I igence received here from Barakhs states that Penjdeh is occupied by a small Russian force, with four guns. The Sarik-Turcomans have bees completely gained over by the Russians. The Afghan troops at Bala Murghab have not received their pay, and are in a somewhat demoralised ewe. The telegraph line has been completed to a point 120 miles beyond Askabad, where there is at presint a lull in the Russian war prepara- tions.

Sr. PETERSBURG,. TRURSIDA.Y.—The Caspian Sea cable has been repaired. The journal GrasUlanin announces that Colonel Z akezevski who arrive! here on the sth inst. with despatches from General.Komaroff proceeded immedia- tely to Gatschina in order to report to the Emperor. The journal adds that according to the information t,rought by Colonel Zakezevski the inhabitants of Penjdeh district are well disposed towards the Russians. The Afghan troops were badly equipped, but their artillery was well served. The Itiovoe Vremye stater; that it has been decided to con- tinue the construction of the Transcaspian Railway beyond Askabah, Kachka, and Mery as far as Burdalik on the Amu Dania. The preparations for the section between Rizil Arvat and Askabad have been already partially made. The other sections will be levelled an once, and the whole line as far as Kachka will be finished towards the end of next autumn. It is added that the co7.tinuation to Mery will be completed in the spring of 1856, while the Section to Burdalik will be constructed in the summer of that year. The general superintendence of the work will be entrusted to General Annenkoff.
LORD TIFNNYiON AND GENERAL
GORDON.
In reply to a letter from the American poet Whittier about General Gordon, Lord Tennyson has written as follows :
"Dear Mr. Whittier,—Your reauest has been forwarded to me, and I herein 8,m4 you an epit ,ph or Gordon in our Westminster Abbey—i e, for his cenotaph :

Warrior of God, man's friend, nnt here below, But romewhere dead far in the waste Soudan ; Thou livest in all hearts, kr all men know Ihis earth lath bore no simpler, nobler man. With best wishes, yours very faithfully. " TENNYSON."

The Rev. john Thomas D.D., of Liverpool, has accepted the chairmanship of the Thomas, Union at the unani- mous request of the committee. THE QUEEN'S VISIT TO THE CONTINENT.-011 Saturday morning Her Majesty the Queen embtrkel on board the royal yacht Victoria and Albert, Captain Fullerton, reach- ing Tort Victoria at 415 p.m.. and travelling thence by special train on the North Kent and South-Western Rail- ways, arriving at Windsor Castle the same evening. The suite in attendance consisted of Lady Churchill. the Dowa- ger Marchioness of Ely, General the Right Hon. Sir H. Ponsonby, K.C.8., Major Edwards, C. 8., and Dr. R. Reid.

LORD SALISBURY IN 114CiN&Y.—Th3 Marvis of S 411&. bury, in epening a new Constrvative club at Hackney on Tuesday, expressed his convic,ion that their principles were spreading in the -borough constituencies. Tber were all reeling under the blow of a terrible budget, which pressed rather upon native industries than upon importations, and would further depress agriculture and increase the heavy burdens on land and house property. Reform of taxation was urgently needed in order to bring in the whole mass of the wealth of the country to bear equally the rates and taxes. What had they got for the fourteen millions of deficit? They heard of hopes of peace and arbitration. Russia had at- tacked our allies and hunted our officers like bares. Trust- worthy engagements with nue,ii were hopeless. We must defend India in the manner Lotd Beaconsfield proposed. Our Government blundered into difficulties with a light heart and escaped from them with a light foot. Examples of this were afforded in Afghanistan, Egypt, and the Soudan. The expenditure of our blood and money was always ren- dered fruitless. People asked "Do you then disagree with the Government's policy? " He replied that they were like a drunken man; he did not disagree with their directs. I tion, but with their reeling from side to side, • •

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN. BURNING OF THE RAILWAY.—ARRIVAL OF LORD I'VOLSELEY.--Sb)BMISSION OF TRIBES. SUAKIM, FRIDAY.—Last night General Graham himself went in the patrol train which rune during the night be- tween Suakin: and Handout) to endeavour to put a stop to attempts upon the HIM. Whie the engine was taking in water at Hendon!), the rebels eel fire to the sleepers in six . plac.s burning them for some two hundred yards. The men at the first look-out station saw large numbers of rebels ;retreating towards II tsheen, and General Graham went out I at daybreak with a cavalry escort to the highest hills of the I range between Haudoub and Hasheen, but no enemy could be seen. During the night some kundreds of shots were fired into the camp at Otao. The Australians. Camel Corps. and Madras Sappers and Miners returned here from Otao this morning. The 74th have ale) come into Suakim, and the 49th will return to-morrow. The Shater Arabs have tendered their enbmission teed-1y at Otao. They can put in the field fifteen hundred fighting men and a branch of the Hadendowa tribr). .n.axim, SATURDAY.—LOrd Wolseley arrived here in the Queen at half-pot three o'clock this afternoon. On land- ing, Lord Wolseley was received with a gnarl of honour of I fifty men of the Grenadier Guards. Lord Wolseley rode through the cutup to head-quarters Ile went on board the Queen again for the night. The pest at Otao was again fired into. The Menthe, who are the principal herders and graziers of cattle in this part of the country, and are like the Shater, a branch-of the Thdendowa trihe, have sent in to say that they are ready to tender their conditional surrender. They number three thousand men, women, and children.

Blzizawr SUNDAY. Colonel Temple, with a troop of Hussars and the Egyptian Caineley, to-day visited the Crasal Wells, lying ten nines to the east of this poet. Ihe walk of hut-building is noiv completed, and the troops are engaged upon the repair of the whale boats. The sick are doing well.

DONGOIA' SUNDAY—News has bees received here con- firrninv the defeat of the Irlabdi's troops at Mesalarnial, near Senaar. It is added that they sustains.' great losses. The rising in Kordofan is spreading, and great distress pre- vails there, owing to the rcarcity of food. DEFEAT OF THE REBEL.-50 KILLED AND 2,000

div.head: CATI'LE CAP I URED.
div.p: CATI'LE CAP I URED.

The Press Asso-cratijn-b-as-re-c.eiC;i.f--;;i the War Office a copy of the following telegram from Lord Wolseley to the Secretary for War, dated Suakim, Wednesday, 10 p.m. : Graham executed a very successful and well-planned raid last night on Takool, a village ten miles south of Otao. and twenty miles west of Suakim. which was occupied by Mah- mined Adam Sardoun, one of Osman Digrna's most impor- tant followers. Sardoun had at Sakool the only organised force remaining in the'fild. which was reported to be 700 strong. Graham started at one am from Suakim with the 9th Bengal Lancers, the Mounted Infantry of the Engineers and Guards, and the Camel Corp?, and, in combination with him, a column left Otao consisting of Mounted Infantry, the 15th Sikhs, and 200 friendlies. Both columns marched on Takool, which they reached shortly after daybreak. Gra- ham's force arriving shortly before the other. They drove the enemy out of Takool, captured between 1,500 and 2,000 sheep and goats, and returned to their respective camps after hiring burnt Takool. The enemy's loss is est'rnated at 50 killed. Our casualties are—Lieutenant A. K. Austin, Shrop- shire Bailment an.l Camel Corps, severely wounded, and two men wounded. Graham reports all the treops as having behaved well.

INSPECTION OF TROOPS. TRURSDAY.—Lord Wolseley when inspecting the troops at Otao and Handub yesterday complimented the Australian artillery and Sikhs on their good appearance, and promised one of the native officers a sword for gallantry. The hired transport Geelong has left for Portsmouth with 150 invalids and 200 navvies on board. THE BOSPHORE INCIDENT. CAIRO, SATURDAT.—The details connected with the re- turn of the French Diplomatic Agent to this city have now been arranged.—MlDNlGHT.--M. Taillandier arrived here at ten o'clock this evening, and was met at the Railway Sta- tion by the Khedive's Master of the Ceremonies and the staff of the French Consulate. Only a few of the French residents were present, and M. Taillandier's reception was lukewarm and without enthusiasm.

Canto, SUNDAY.—Nubar Pasha has paid a visit to M. Tal- landier, the acting French DTI omatic Agent, and expressed the regret of the Egyptian Government at the incident attending the suppression of the Bosphore Egypte:en. M. Taillandier subsequently returned the visit. CAIRO, TUESDAY.—Coostquent upon the remonstrances of Sir Evelyn Baring, M. Taißendier, the artmg French diploreat,c agent, has undert.ken that the Bosphore Egyptieni shall not he republished uutll he has received in.Vuctions from his Government in the matter. FRANCE AND CHINA. PARIS, SATURDAY.—A telegram dated here from Hanoi of to-day's date, states that the evacuation of Tonquin by the Chinese continues, and that the Imperial troops have now uil.t commenced retreating he Red River. PARIS, WRDNRSDAY.—Thelfinistry of War has received a despatch from General Briere de dated Hanoi, yes- terday, stating that the retreat of the bhin-er,?, troops con- tinues on the Red River, although the movement is ducted slowly.____

THE NEW CONGO STATE. Bnusssts, MuNnev.—The deputation, comprising the Lord Mayor of London, Alderman Sir Thomas Dakin, Sir Thomas 'Chambers, Mr. Alderman de Keyser, Mr. Sheriff Whitehead, Mr. Sheriff Paudel Phillips, Sir John IWonckton, Mr. Dresser Rogers, and Mr. Deputy Bedford, WAS received this morning by King Leopold, te whom they presented a congratulatory address. His Majesty afterwards invited the deputation to dine it the Castle, at Lacken. The mem- bers of the deputstion, in the course of the day, visited the Hotel de Ville and the Palais de Justice.

THE UNITED STATES.—FATAL FIRE.—STRIKE RIOT; TWO KILLED. NEW YORK, SIINDAY.—A fire broke out in a tenement house in this city last night, resulting in the death of nine persons throush suffocation or from injuries received in the panic which ensued on the alarm of fire being raised. A number of other persons were also hurt. NESS' YORK, Mc NDAY.—A strike has occurred among the quarrymen at Lemont, Illinois. The men assembled to-day- and assumed a threatening attitude, necessitating the inter— foronce of the military. The troops ultimately fired upon the meb, killing two persons and wounding several.

THE RISING IN CANADA. OTTAWA, SUNDAY.—RieI has issu d a proclamation, in which he tells the half-breeds who have hitherto refused to join him that they must come immediately or he will mur• der them. The troops are gradually surrounding the rebel Indians is Battleford and the Edmonton region. Orraws, MONDAY —Riel's runn•rs have met with no suc- cess in their endeavours to incite the Indians and half- breeds in Qu'Appelle region to rebellion, and have returned crestfallen. A speedy collapse of the rebalion is expec- ted. _

ENGAGEMENT WITH THE REBELS. OrrAwA, WRDNNSDAY.—lntellizence received here states that an engagement took place at Battleford on Sunday last between 300 Canadian troops and 100 Indians owing allegi- ance to the Chief Poundrnaker. The troops loot seven killed and 12 wounded, while the Indian loss was SO killed and wounded. CIVIL WAR IN PERU. LIMA, SATMIDAY.—The Government troops have ben defeated at Ayacucho. General Caceres is marching upon Lima, and preparations are being made for a great battle in the vicinity. The Peruvian National Assembly has been prorogued. THE SUEZ CANAL CONFERENCE. nuts, THURSDAY.—The Suez Canal Commission has commenced the discussion of the French proposals for en- trusting an international body, similar to the Danube Com- mission, with the control and supervision of the free naviz,a- tion of the Canal. Tbe proposal is supported by the Ger- man. and opposed by the British h Austrian,an d It a lai annd delegates. Russian decision has yet been arrived at, the discussion baying hitherto been of a prelimi- nary character.

In the London Sheriff's Court on Thursday a jury as- sessed the damages at £lO,OOO in the action brought by Mrs. Weldon against M. Ciounod for libel, slander, breach of con- tract, and assaelt. Lieutenant-Colonel Kennedy, who commanded the Cana- dia n voyageurs during their duties en the Nile, and who died a few days ago in London, was buried at Highgate Cemetery on Wednesday. to murder a young A labourer named Baugh was remanded cm Wednesday at p.etrirliguto the canal, after ng her. womanWb roltvaellryttnaaammsspeatdoolnjt iocyhcaer g:yd withthrowing att emi The annual general meeting of the Iron and Steel Institute was opened on Wednesday at the Institution of 1 Civil lingineers, London, Sir Birnhard Samuelson, M.P., ' presiding. It Was stated that the Bessemer medal had been awarded to Professor IL A. Kerman, of Stockholm. DESTRUCTIVE FIRE.—A fire broke out at an early boar on Wednesday morning on the extensive premises of Messrs. Jackson and Graham, upholsterers and furnishing ware- housemen, Oxford-street and Newman-street, London. The damece, which is covered by Insurance, is estimated at from £40,000 to £50,000. _ . _

- --Speaking in London on Wednesday evening, Mr. Trevel• van said the stormy cloud of foreign politics had been sud he' hoped within the past few days materially lightened, that it would soon clear off altogether, though it was not yet the time for congratulating each other or for relaxing Our vigilance and preparation. fiRRACtr or Pnomrsz.—An action to recover damages 'o- at a Sheriff'e Court in breach of promise of marriage was beard on Wednesday jury Ylizabeth Dorothy Graham, of before Pre- ston. ease:ls:it:it; jai; dwauj Littleborough, and the defendant David Edmund Lewis, of Workington. The breach was admitted, and the jury asses- sed the damages at £l5O, with costs. Mumma OF A CONSTABLR —The trill Of MOM Shrimp- ton for the murder of Police Constable Davies at Alvechurch concluded-on Thursday at Worcester Assizes. The indict- ment rested upon evidence which was purely cirOUrclitan' Val, but which so nearly approached the nature of direct proof that the jury found their verdict of "guilty" after a merely formal retirement of a few minutes' duration. Shrimpton, whose capture within a few hours of the murder was a distinct testimony to the acuteness of the loci' police, received his sentence of death calmly, but declared that ha was innocent. Mary Morton, the woman arraigoed with him as an accessory after the fact, was acquitted.

fessed to be a County Court process when it was nothing of the kind ; and, as there was nothing for it but to plead guilty in face of the evidence against him, the prisoner was sentenced to ten years' penal servitude. His lordship commented on the fact that O'HARA had undoubted ability, and that he had been a member of a noble and honourable profession for twenty-five years. It transpired that the prisoner had previously been sentenced at Belfast to twelve months' imprisonment, and that for the first six months of his incarceration he pretended to be deaf and dumb. It appears that during the past week he resorted to the same tac- tics; but he went beyond this, for he put an end to his life by converting a towel into a cord and hanging himself. Such startling cases as these bring home to everybody the truth of the proverb as to honesty being the best policy. Had O'HARA continued in the straight path—content to " labour and to wait "—he would long since have overcome his financial difficulties, and, instead of perishing in gaol, he would still have been a member of "a noble and honourable pro- fession."

This has become a truism, as it relates to the amenities of the street ; but the world is as yet so barbarous in its inter- national relations that the custom as yet is to fight first and reason afterwards. It thus happens that when, as in this instance, the right thing is being done, "fellows of the baser sort" expose themselves by talking of cowardice and surrender. Lord R. CHURCH- ILL did attempt to give something like sub- stance to his vapourings by saying "he greatly feared that we might have lost India." He might just as well have said he greatly feared Russia might have lost Siberia. Upon finding that his ridiculous statement excited laughter, he tried to explain that when he said lost he didn't mean lost, leaving the House to infer that it was the speaker himself who was lost. He was more successful when he set himself to the task of showing that Russia was advancing s'ep by step in Central Asia, and that she was not to be relied upon I in the promises that she made.
