Russia must certainly be kept out of Afghanistan; but, having annexed Turkistan, it is undeniable that her frontier now extends to that of the territory of the AMBER. The delimitation of that frontier is desirable —it is absolutely necessary before we or the AMBER can say—" Thus far shalt thou go, but no further." It is to this end that the British Government are labour- ing ; and in drawing the line of demaication regard must be had to the wishes of the AmEER and of Russia—especially when their wishes coincide, Mr. GLLIDSTONS is WO pru- dent and too just to force territory upon the Afghans which they may not be willing to receive ; but once let the frontier be defi- nitely determined, Russia will then know that to violate it will be as dangerous as a viola- tion of the frontier of India. Meantime, England and Russia, heving perilous dif- ferences, are doing that which is wise and honourable and an example to the world; they are referring the matter of their dispute to arbitration, and the result is that— Grim-visaged. war hath smoothed his wrinkled front while a peace is promised which is in the nature of a conquest

nix Manchester ship canal Bill passed the Committee of the House of Lords on Thursday; and the event has caused the liveliest satisfaction in Manchester and throughout this district. Even those who remain as yet to be convinced of the practi- cability of the scheme feel that the promoters have done all that could be reasonably expected of them in order to meet the exigen- cies of the situation, and that they are en- titled to be permitted to go forward with their venture. Their lordships have shown business-like tact and decision in dealing with the evidence which has been brought before them, and, without slighting any issue, they have aimed at saving the time and money ot those engaged in the case. The bill passes the Lords' Committee subject, as last year, to a clause requiring the promoters to raise £5,000,000 before the works are commenced a provision which, though it may have its drawbacks in the first instance, will make the way easy after the initial difficulty is overcome. It was intimated that their lordships were disposed to impound the deposit of four per cent. upon the canal portion of the works; but on Mr. PEMBER urging the hardship to the pro- moters of locking up the £2,56,00s which had been raised, the Committee decided not to insist upon this condition. Some reference was made to this feature of the decision at the meeting of the Mersey Dock Board on Thursday. The members who were present obviously spoke under the impression —de- rived no doubt from the first telegrams—that the deposit was to be impounded; but they will have learned since the meeting that the promoters are not to be held to this onerous condition. It will now be for the Commons' Committee to consider the bill. There is a growing feeling that it will pass that body, too, notwithstanding that it was adverse to the scheme of last year. It is much to be regretted that it should be necessary for private bills to go before two Committees ; but it would seem that Lords and Commoners are like oil and water—they will not mix. The new Parliament will be called upon, amongst other things, to find a way out of this difficulty; for commercial men, irrespec- tive of party, are growing more and more impatient of extravagant and antiquated modes of doing business.

ATTEMPTED SPICIDE AT FRODSAAM BRIDGE. At the Occasional Court House, F odsham, on Saturday, Clif- ford Scott Hoskin was charged before Mr. E. A. Wright with attempting to Commit suicide at Frodsham Bridge, on the I‘t inst., by cutting his tkroat. Margaret Duocalf deposed that on Fri- day afb.rneon she saw the prisoner corns out of an outhouse near her house at Frodsham Bridge. He had blood at his throat and on his hands and dress. He followed her to- wards her house, and then turned off along the river side. She followed him as far as Ashworth's bone works, when Mr. Earlam asked the prisoner if he would wash himself, and he did so with the assistance of several persons.—')r. Weaver said a few minutes after five o'clock on the previous day the prisoner was brought to his surgery by A police- constable. There was a quantity of blood about his neck and chest, sad a wound on the left aide of the throit It WAS an incised wound about two and a half inches long, cutting through the skin to the tissues beneath, and was more than half an inch deep. In the deepest part it w-tis about three-quarters of an inch deep. It was a jigged wound, but the great blood vessels and the windpipe were not cut. The wound was such as might have been inflicted by the knife produced. The prisoner handed the papers produced to the witness at his surgery, and said ‘• You see I meant to do it, and I wrote this for my wife," pointing eat the pencil writing on the paper. which was as follows : " Ist of May, 1885. My dear wife.—lf you will not see- me alive, you will see me dead.—Yours truly, C. S. Hes- kin." The prisoner was committed for trial at the Chester Sessions. INGSNIOLD FRADD MT A WIDNES RAILWAY PORTER.— At Widnes Police Court on Wednesday James Kenyon was brought up on remand charged with stealing three return I half tickets from Liverpool to Ditton on the 2nd May, the property of the London and North-Western Riilway Com- pany. He was also charged with having travelled from I Liverpool to Ditton without having previously paid his fare.—Mr. Preeton, Juno, of Lime-street Station, prosecuted. He said the prisoner was a porter in the service of the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Con:piny at Ditton Junc- tion, and was well acquainted with the routine ef the station. On the 2nd May he went to the young porter who was collecting tickets, and asked him if he had any " return halts" from Liverpool to Dittos. The collector answered "No, I have nipped them all and put them away." At that moment three passengers were corning up the stairs, and the prisoner said, " Wait a minute. Let's see where these people are from." These persons delivered up return halts from Liverpool to Ditton, and immediately afterwards the prisoner snatched them out of the young porter's hand and ran away. Later in tke day the prisoner and two other persons delivered up thse, tickets, having travelled by train from Live-pool to ()Won Junction. The wiaoner very well knew that if he had ex- posed these tickets at Lime-street they would not be pagsed, so he cunningly took tickets from Lime-street to Edge 11111, which he showed to the collector on the platform, acid was thus enabled to enter the train. Mr. Preston referred to the serious nature of the offences. and ctliel Vf itnesses in sup- port of his statement. —Ernest William Stanford, detective sergeant on the railway, deposed to apprehending the pri- soner, who, in answer ta the charge, said " I got them (the tickets) out of the booking office off the rack • whilst the clerk was going to his tea. I don't think anyone saw me get them. The boy was collecting at the door."—For travel- ling without a ticket the prisoner was fined 103 and costs, or 14 days.—Mr. Gasketl characterised the charge of theft as a very serious offence, and the prisoner was ordered to pay a penalty of £5 and costs, or go to gaol for a =oath.

A FAMILY Drsrurn AT Ruaconte.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Mon lay, Edward Johnson, a labourer, was awn- mooed for assaulting Sarah Jane Bet's. Mr. Barton de- fended.—The complainant stated that she had purchased a washhaml stand and dressing table and placed them at her mother's house. On her mother's death her sister seized them. At half-past seven on the morning of the 29th, the defendant, who is her brother-iv-law, and lived in Shaw- street, was removing his furniture. She asked him for the table, and he replied that he would" hit her in the mouth," following up his worde by knocking her to the ground and knelt upon her. He and his wife then " knocked her " :about shamefully, and she had scarcely been &de to move elucc..—Witnest-es supported this statement. —William Nor- folk, carter, Ellesmere-street, who had bzen subpecied, de- posed that he was removing the defendant's furniture. The plaintiff came up to the door and used most filthy language to the defendant and his wife. She tkreatenea to break the table to bits,!and the article wao consequently taken back into the house. Shortly afterwards the defendant was bringing a mattress out, when the complainant sprang at him, struck him twice on thn face and fiald her fingers in his hair, and he was with difficulty released from her grasp. The defendant never struck her at all —Several witnesses corroborated this statement.--George Betts, hushind of the complainant iu the last case, was then summoned for assaulting Edward Johnson. Mr. Burton representtd John- son —lt was alleged that on Thursday Johnson was walking down the street with two pictures under hie arm, when the defendant struck him on the ear an knocked his hat off.— The defendant stated he only " s'oved hint."—A namber of witnesses were heird.--Miriam Johnson, wife of Edward Johnson, summoned Ann Walley for art assault on Friday, the Ist inst.—lt was alleged that the defendant asked the complainant to rive up the table and struck her on the lace. —The defence was that the complainant made use of °pore- bioas epithets and that the defendant only put her fist to the complainant's free, but 4id not strike her. She sAhl " Only for the law she would warm her."—The Bench dis- missed the case against Johnson ; fined George Betts is and costs, 12s ; and Ann Walley is and costs, 15s 61. The magistrate remarked that the case against Betts was a foolish and trumpery one.

FOUND DEAD AT RUNCORN.—Mr. T. J. Ridgway, coroner for the honeur and fee of Halton, held an inquest at the 'Police Court, Runcorn, on Kmday, on the body ef Bertha Dutton, infant child of Peter Dutton, dock labourer, of 4, Pool-lane. The child, which was six weeks old, bad en- joyed good health from birth. On Friday night there was a slight blue appearance about its mouth, but it took its food willingly and Mrs. Dutton retired with it to rest about eleven o'clock. She awakened several times during the night and attended to the wants of the infant, who appeared In its usual condition. At seven o'clock, however, when she arose, the child was detd, its hands being tightly clenend. It was not black.—Mrs. Elizabeth Hedgcock, of St. Jobs-street, who bad laid out the infant, deposed that the body was well nourished and well cared for; Mrs. Dut- ton took care of her children. She thought. the child had died from convulsions.—The jury, at the suggestion of the coroner, returned a verdict of " Found dead," SHOCKING DEATH AT WIDNES.—James Yarwood, 24, chemical labourer, who lived at 9, Caroline-street, Widnes, died on Thursday evening under the following circum- stances. On Monday, the 12th January, Yarwood was at Messrs. Muspratts' Liverpool Works, assisting ia the erec- tion of a chamber." The mason, named Barrett, was on the top of the chamber, and Yarwood was standing on the ground near the erection, when by some means a large rope fell from the top upon his head. Although there were no external marks of injury, be complained very much of pains in his head, and on the following day he cime to his home at Widnes. In a fortnight he had lost his eyesight, and he was taken to the Liverpool Eye and Ear Institution. lie was there attended by Dr. Brown, but he became wortle, and was eventually removed to the Royal Infirmary in Dover-street. He remained in that institution until the 15th April, when he was bought home, and died as above stated. He was atten3led in Widnes by Drs. Cooper and Pattison. The coroner ha's been notified.

ALLEGED KIDI•TAPPING AT HALEROOD.—At the Wollton Petty Sessions, on Friday, a respectable locking man named Richard Kirkby, living at Halebank, was summoned for child-stealing at Halewood on Sunday, the 19th ult. Mt. Quil Ham appeared to prosecute ; and Mr. J. 0. Swift de- fended. The child in question. whoee parents are both dead, was named Eden Florence Grace, aged about six•years, and she resided with her grandmother OA her father's side at Halewood. On Sunday, the 19th ult., the child was play- ing in a field at Halewood, when the defendant, who was her uncle on her mother's side by marriage, went into the field and carried her oft —Mr. Quintana said that under those circumstances, unless the child were given up, he would ask the magistrates to commit the defendant to the EVIiZ `a —Mr. Swift suggested that an arrangement might be made, and in this the Bench concurred. After some con- sultation between Mr. Quilliam and Mr. Swift, it was agreed t6at the child should reside alternately with the two families. and that the present summons should be with- drawn. .

div.p: SALE OF WORK AT WIDNES.

Yesterdey a sale iim;;;;s -c-o-mr.nven-ced-h-e.the National Schools, Waterloo-road, in aid of the building fund of St. Paul' Church, Anderson's-corner. It will be remembered .that about twelve months ego a committee of the parishioners 'guaranteed to either =tribute Cr raise the sum of £l,OOO towards the cost of the erection of the edifice, and of this amount they have now paid into bank £9OO. By this sale of work, which consists principally of goods unsold at the bazaar held in winter, it is expected that the total amount of the guarantee will be reached. There was no formal , opening ceremony. The stalls were presided over by the following ladies :—(1) Mrs. Williams, Mrs. Kilcross, Cave, and Miss Wilkinson; (2) Mrs. Lord, Mrs. While, Mrs. Neil, and Miss Gill ; (31 Mrs. 'nelson. Mrs. Crawford, Mrs. Wharton, Mrs. Hunt, and Mrs. Crabtree ; (refreshments) Mrs. Pemberton, Mrs. C. Davics, and Mrs. Park.,.—Mr. Lord exhibited various interesting optical instruments, and Mr. Foley, the lay reader, bad arranged a museum of Indian and Chinese curiosities, which he had collected during his sojourn abroad. The Rev. C. Rumfit was the curator of a fine art gallery. During the evening concerts and minst•el entertainments took place.

HEAVY DEATH RATE AT RUNCORN. In the first quarter of this year there was a fcrther in- crease in the mortality of the town and sub-district of Run- corn, for the deaths were 151 against 98 in last December. These 151 deaths corresponded to an annual rate of 307 per 1,000 of the population, estimated to be, in the middle of this year 20,359, showing an increase of 1,156 on the total enumerated at the last census. That death-rate was a very high one, as it was 101 more than that of the 50 great towns in England and Wales. Runcorn had a much higher rate than Widnes. The latter is included in the sub•dis- trict of Farnworth, and it is assumed that this year it will have 32,031 i.habit ants, being a growth of 4,336 on the number in 1881. The deaths in it were 118, and these yielded a rate of 144, which %%le 15.8 less than that of Run- corn. In Liverpool the rate was 25.5, in Birkenneati 18'G, in Warrington 192, and in Chester 21.9 ; so that the 302 in 114ncorn was greater than any of these. In fact, among the 78 great towns in England and Wales there wete but three of them with a higher rate. In the third period of 1884 Runcorn suffered a great deal from diarrheas, which was fatal in 40 cases ; besides, there were 7 each of scarlet fever and fever. In the December period the first of these was not represented, but fever was credited with 8. Of these 8 deaths, 5 (typhoid) occurred in the Urban Sanitary district. In the present return there was a severe outbreak of measles, which was fatal in 31 cases, and there were besides 1 each of smallpox and diarrheet, and 2 of fever. The 151 deaths in Runcorn in the first three months of this year comprised 77 males, and 74 females ; and of the total 41 were those of infants under one year, and 24 re- ferred to adults who had attained 63 years and upwards. There were six deaths due to violence, and inquests were bed on 10 bdies. The births in the town and stab-district numbered 207, and these included 101 boys and 106 girls. In June last there were 211. The births in the sub-district cf Frodsham, which includes Kingsley as well as Frodsham, were 50; and as the deaths numbered 42. there were 11 more than what was anticipated. In last December the latter were 36, but in the preceding September only 20. Bud- worth sub-district had 41 births and 23 deaths ; Daresbury, 27 and 19 ; Widnes and Farnworth, 310 aril 118 ; and War- rington, 463 and 231 respeetively. In all of them the mor- tality was low.

The second team bad played 20 matches, 140! which they had won, 3 lost, and 3 drawn. (Applause.) The committee could only point to a slight improvement on last year's results of matches, and had again to complain of members failing to turn up when they had b3en selected to play. This was especially noticeable ! in the matches played away from biome, the majo:ity of which were lost and drawn. The resole of some of Om ; matches would have catainly been different had the teams ; been more represeetative. (Hear, hear.) These remarks were applicable only as the first team. (Applause.) Since the last meeting the club had removed ! to a new field, and although the outlay h id bean very heavy, it was heped the club would real, the benefit hereafter. There was an increase in the gate money of £'ls , Ili 41 upon previous vears—kaoplause)—and next year it was expected the club would be &all to pay the players , full railway fares, and bear all o;ber expenses incurred by them. Stirrup ; sub-captain, Mr. T. Bingham ; Mr. Ashall, treasurer ; Mr. Brown, secretary ; Mr. F. Wright, as&istant secretary ; committee, Messrs. Ricaarda, Ireland. div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. _
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. _

The monthly meetihg was held on Thursday, Mr. J. Meadowcroft presiding. Present—Messrs. Norman, Dobson, Grice, Whittaker Speakman, Lake, Taylor, White, Wil- liams, E. Marshall (secretary), M. Barker (surveyor).
THE MEDICAL REPORT.

The Medical Officer reported that the number of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 46. Of these deaths 12 were caused by bronchitis, 10 measles, 3 cardiac disease, 3 natural decay, 2 paralysis, 2 ganerene ; scarlatina, pthisis, abscess, dropsy, brain Liver, meningitis, apoplexy, defective nutrition, dentition, corrosion of stomach, and septiclina account for one each. Of the above deaths, 27 occurred amongst children 10 years and under, and 10 of these were under one year, making a death rate of 28.9 per 1,000 of the population per annum—ln answer to questions, Dr. Mouritz said measles wire dying out, and Mr. Dobson stated that nearly all the chddren had gone back te school.

div.head: HIGHWAY HATTERS.
div.p: HIGHWAY HATTERS.

IThe Hiehway and Sanitery Committee had reeolved that ne scavenging plant (sub) committee with Mr. Norman, attend the sales of Mrs. Sefton an Mr. Thomas Cliffe, and purchase such scavenging plant as they might deem expe- dient. It was decided that a scavenging foremen be enga- ged by the surveyor at wages 22s per we k. The Local Government Board had written pointing out that as the Commissioners desired to receive repayment fur the Parlia- mentary grant on account of the salery of the Inspector of Nuisances, the appointment of this effacer had not teen made in conformity with the provisions of the General Order of the 10th of March, 1880, and that it will be nem. wary to proceed formally to appoint an officer after due notice given by advertisem.nt, purenant to article 0 of the Order.—The Secretary was instructed to cemply with the requirements of the Local Government Order.—The minutes were adopted on the motion of Mr. Nortuen.-1 he Canal Boats and Hospital Committee reselved that the draft of the Public notice to owneie and masters of canal boats regietered at Runcorn, that a distinctive mirk be no longer required, and drawing their attentioa to the provisions of the Canal Boats act, 1884, be approved and recommended to the Board for adoption.—Tbe Survevor reported that the time for completing the hospital coutract expired on the 20th March last, and that the contractor wee liable to a penalty of five pounds for every week that the work remains unfinished from that time.—lt was recommended that four iron beds and necessary window blinds for the new ward in the hospital be purchased.—Mr. Dobson moved the adoption of the minutes and said that a cheque for £75 had been ordered to be signed for Mr. Sta- tham on account of the hospital contrect. He had since made application for a further .£l5, and Mr. Barker said as the work was far advanced the Board would be justified iu the payment. lie therefore moved that addition to the minutes.—Mr. P. Speakman seconded the motion.— The Chairman, reTerring to the hospilal, deprecated rnnnir into extravagant and unnecessary expenditure, and sugge ted that furniture and bedding should be provided as cl cumstances required it. Besides, there was very litl probability of the place being required —Mr. Barker, answer to questions, slid there had only been one patie Ito the hospital since it was erected. There were fcur be there at the present time.—Mr. Lake was in favour of flit' and furnishing the building, and Mr. Grice said now tt hod got the hospital he thought they ought to have properly fitted up.—Mr. linker retnaleed that smallpox was very prevalent in Manchester and Selford. Be did net know whether the disease would visit Runcorn or not. —The minutes were adopted.

div.head: MARKET.
div.p: THE MARKET.

The Market Superintendent reported to the General Pur- poses Committee that the receipts for the past month amounted to £2B 19s 10J, being an increase of £5 143 Id as the corresponding period last year. During the corret• ponding period last year nine shops were unoccupied, while at the present time there were i.nly two in that condition. —The minutes were adopted on the motion of Mr. Dobson seconted by Mr. Norman,

div.head: FINANCES.
div.p: THE FINANCES.

The Finance Committee --reported that the receipts for April amounted to SAI 5s 31. Accunts ameunting to £315 Is 2d were passed for payment. The follmaing is a list of the treasurer's balance—District fund Is 2.1, unepent loan £1,425 3 a 3d, sinking fund £133 IN 93, general fund over. draft £203 183 41 It was resolved that the security given by the surveyor and collector be increased from £75 to £4OO, and that the secretary and sccmntant give security In the sum of £2OO ; bonds to be obtained in each from the London Guarantee Society; and th:t the sum of £2 10s be remitted to the Public Library Committee, consiquent upon the pro:nised reduction of rent whenever the overseers corn- mrncsd to pay full rent for the offices occupied by them in the Town Hall.—Mr. Norman moved that the minutes pass with the exception of that relating to the Free Library Committee.—The gscretary said it was an arrangement that when the overseers paid full rent the rent paid by the Library Committee should be reduced, but the overseers only came on full rent in March.—Mr. Lake remarked that the overseers had paid something iik 3£6 up to March, but the Board had been receiving rent from Mr. Coleburn for the old overseers' offices. Tale he argued was equivalent to the overseers paying full rent, and he csntended that the Library Committee was entitled to the reduction. He moved that the minute be referred blck to the Committee. —Mr. Norman accepted this motion, and the minutes passed.

div.head: SHIP CANAL SCHEME.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL SCHEME.

The minutes of the Parliamentary and Legal Committee contained the following :—Letter from Mr. S. C. Beckett forwarding resolutions passed at a meeting of the merchants and tradesmen of Runcorn. It was resolved that in addition to Mr. Fisher and Mr. Tuft, Captains Anderson and Paul. together with any other suitable persons (the selection to ho left to the Chairman and the Law Clerk) be asked to giver evidence in favour ot the Commissioners' clause', and that the Law Clerk should prepare their evidence as s.)on as pos- sible. On April 18th Messrs. Graham, Curry, and spec, pointing out that the chief opponents of the Ship Canal Bill contemplated withdrawing further opposition, it was resolved that such expenses be aliowed Captains Hill and Shaw, if they were required in London to give evidence, as the deputation thought desirable.—The minutes were ad- opted, on the motion of Mr. Speakman, seconded by Mr. Dobson.

- - PUBLIC FOUNTAINS To BE ERECIT.D. The Public Fountains Committee recommended that drink- ing fountains be erected near the Police Station and at Delph Bridge, and that two drinking fountains be purchased from Messrs. Walter MacFarlane and Company, Glasgow, at a cost of El 9s 6d and El 3s 31 respectively. The Runcorn. Weston, and Halton Water Works Company stated that they could not supply water for the use of the drinking fountains at less than their usual rate ; and the committee therdore- recammencled that two water meters be purchased from the IS Runcorn, Weston, and Halton at :a. Works Company, at a cost of £2 123 each.-Mr. D!lbson, in moving the ackotion of the minutes, said the committee hal caret Lila- considered this matter, end the total cost of the fountains Would not exceed £l5 173 91.—Mr. Taylor seconded the motion.— Mr. Lake said re thought drinking troughs for animals almost more important than drinking fountains, and he would rather sea one drinking foustain coup'ed with a trough for ani nals than two fountains with- out provision for animals. lie doubted the necessity of a drioking fountain at Delph Bridge and another at the Mar- ket, the distance was so short. He suggested that it would be b.tter to fix one near Top Locks.—Mr. Dobson said this question of providing for the animals had not escaped the notice of the committee. They had considered the erection of a fountain in Devonshire-square with a trough for ani- mals, but for financial reasons no reconatnendation was made to the Board.—Mr. Speakman congratulated the . movers in this matter, and expressed his pleasure that the monument opposite the Town Hall would serve a utilitarian purpose in the future.—The Chairman thought this a step in the right direction, but there was another step that was equally important, and that was the. erection of puhlic urinals. (Hear, hear.) He ho!eed this work would be car- ried out by the present Committee. Mr.Dolason re- marked that provision had been made for carrying out this work in the estimates,—The Chairman was of opinion that drinking troughs for animals were nor greatly needed in a place like Rune ,rn, where the road traffic was not heavy.— Mr. Dobson agreed to endeavour to make provision for a drinking trough for dogs, and he accepted a le-lotion of Mr. Lake's that the committee consider the advisability of providing drinking troughs for animals.—The minutes were passed. There was nil other business of public interest.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

%ARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATnianay.—Tha hipiness is reported in another column. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Coun- cillor Greening, and Mr. John Fairclough. MISCELLANEOUS.—The following charges of drunkenness were dealt with :—John Lee, in Winwick-street, on Satur- day evening, fined 53. including costs ; William Lewis, a soldier, in Battermarket-street, en Sunday evening, fined ss, including costs; John Woods, in the Market Hall, on the 24th April, fined 53 and costs; James Devaney, in Turner-street, on the 27th April, finrd 5s and costs ; Ann Chsetterton, in Foundry-street, on the 27th ult, fined 53 and costs ; BriJget Higgios, in Buttermarket-street, on the 29th ulr., sent to prison for a month; Martha Cotton, in Dial-street, fined 5s and costs.--James Langley was charged with keening lodgers without having his house registered, on the 29th ult. The house is adapted for five persons and living there eight were found. Defendant woe ordered to pay as 01, the costi.—Joseph Griffiths, for having more lodgers in his house than he was registered for, was fined 5s and costs, or seven days' imprisonment. —Richard Forbes and William Hoyle were ordered to be bound over to keg the peace for six months on a charge of having com- mitted a breach of the peace by fighting, on the 25th ult.— Frank Wilson was ordered to -pay costs for furiously driving a horse and cab in Liverpool-road, en the 23rd Mt. ASSAULT.—Ja.rne3 Powell was charged with assaulting Martin Lalley in Buttermarket-street, on the previous even- ing. Defendant dealt complainant a severe blow under the ear daring the progress of a row. He was fined lOs and costs. Assisrixo TIIE POLlCE.—Patrick Burke was charged with disturbing the peace by fighting in Buttermarket-street, and assaulting P.C. Foams. When the constable was taking prisoner into custody. a soldier named Thompson gave timely assistance, and the Hmc'a complimented him on his action. Burke was bound over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO, and one surety of £5. DnuNic IN A TEAlN.—Edward Joyce was charged with 'being drunk in a railway carriage on the Cheshire Lines Railway, at the Central station, on Saturday. He was found laid on the se it of the carriage and was very violent when asked for his ticket. Fined 103 and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment-. TUESDAY —Before Councillor C. Broadbent and Mr. E.

J. Guest DEIVNICENNESS.—James Walsh, last from Liverpool, and Martin Gleeson, last from Hanley, ressrve men, were charged with being drunk and disorderly on the day pre- vious.—They we-e dismissed. AsstrLY. William Woods was summoned by John Featherstone, labourer, for asqaulting him on the 28th ult. Complainant said that at 11-30 o'clock on the evening of that day be waslin Ellesmere-street, when defendant made an opprobious remark to him. Complainant asked him what he meant and in reply defendant gave him a blow in the face. Afterwards defendant hurled him into the middle of, the road and assaulted him unmercifully.—Mr. Davies ap- peared for the defendant, who endeavoured to make it appear thnt he was not the aggretsor.—The Bench cAnsidered the bvidencs that was given an conflicting as not to justify a conviction, and therefore discharged the defendant. Mr. Z. Armitage. MISCELLANEOUS —Betsy Ellison was charged with assault- ing Agnes Broadhurst on the first inst. She was ordered to be bound over to be of good behaviour for six months.-- Thomas Hunt was charged with threatening his wife, Eliza- beth, on the sth inst. She said that be knocked her about and threatened to kill her; and be alleged that she got drunk and gave him great provocation. Defendant was ordered to be bound over for six months, himself in £lO, and one surety of £lO --Mary Jane Steel was fined 7s. 6d , including costs, for keeping a dog without a license, at Latchford, on the 27th ult.

PERUISSION TO SELL —Mrs. Rigby, widow of the late Mr. Robert Rigby, was granted permission to sell at the London and North-Western Hotel, Lovvlands-road. Bryan and Cooper proved the case, and Farrell was fined Is, and costs lOs 6,L—The other defendants did not appear, and warrants were granted for their apprehension. DRUNK.—EIIen McDonald, for being drunk and incapable ire Charch-street on the 2nd inst, was, on the evidence of P.C. Fryer, sentenced to 14 days bard labour in default of paying a doe of 10s and costs.

DRUNERITNESS.—For this offence John Hughes (Bth appearance), Anthony McGloyne (10. h appearance), Pat- sick Morris, Thomas Handley, Thomas Mullen, Thomas Hulme,Roger Murray, and Patrick Carr were each fined in various amounts. Sinclair, John Stead, a nurseryman, residing at Bold, was charged with being drank and disorderly in Church-street, St. Helens, at six o'clock on Saturday night. On being asked if be was guilty or not guilty, the prisoner said : I might as well plead guilty as not. It was more excitement than anything else.—P.c. McHenry deposed that at the time stated the prisoner was very drunk in charge of a horse and trap and was entirely unable to take charge of the horse.— Superintendent Johnston : What had he in his possession ? —P.C. McHenry : He had a six-chambered revolver, which was loaded in four chambers and had two emp,y cartridges in the remaining barrels.—The Bench imposed a fine of los and costs, or, in default, 14 days' imprisonment.

On the motion of Mr. Dennett, seconded by Mr. Makin, and supported by the Chairman, Mr. Castle Spenceley was appointed .chairman for the ensuing year. The seal of the Board was ordered to be affixed to the new local board rate of Is. 4d. in the £ for the next half year, and Dr. E. F. Hall, medical officer, and Mr. Dickinson, nuisance inspector, were re-elected for another year. Dr. Hall submitted his annual report, which showed that the health and sanitary condition of Prescot was improving. The report stated, as a curious coincidence, that the number of births during the last year was exactly the same as in 1833, again giving a birth-rate of 364 per 1,000 of the population ; the death rate being 18 per 1,000. The total number of blithe for the year was 234, and deaths 116. This was the principal business.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

Since the close of last cricket season there has been for- med a Lancashire Amateur Cricket Association, the object of which is 'to provide a thoroughly representative ama- teur cricket team for the county, and penerally to increase the popularity of the game and encourage the bringing out of local talent." The means adopted to secure this end have been the offering of a challenge cup for competition amongst the club's forming the association. Up to the pre- sent the association has a membership of 18, and these have been drawn together as in football competitions, and the first round has tO be played off on or before the 23rd inst. Arrangements are being made for a visit in the autumn of a team of Devonshire cricketers to the United States. It is sought to arrange matches bath in New York and Phil- adelphia. It is a question of "gate money," and on the egoepects of a series of matches being sufficiently attractive to prove remunerative entirely depends the completion of the tour. The two days' match between the Colts of Yorkshire and Notte, at Trent Bridge, ended in a draw. For Notts G. Bean made 72, T. Lindley 54, and M. Wright 58, the three top scoree. On the side of Yorkshire H. Lee was not die- peed of until be had made 141, a remarkable score, with only two chances; H. Leadbeater was next with 61.—The Seniors' match at Oxford ended on Saturday thus: Money- Wigram's side, 173 and 127; A. E. Newton's side, 117 and 71. In the second innings of the latter Arnall took eight wickets for 32 runs, while Le Messurier, at cover point, dismissed three batsmen in sncoession.—ln a trial match at the Oval (Surrey County Club) between sides captained respectively by W. W. Read and J. Shuter, Bowley, the ex- Northamptonshire professional, took six wickets for 54 runs.—The contest, Army v. Navy, at Portsmouth, ended in favour of the former by 152 runs to 88 The Burnley cricket season was opened on Saturday with a match against Bury. The attendance was good, the receipts being £5 more than was obtained at the same match last year.—Werneth and Huddersfield tried conclusions, on the ground of the latter, on Saturday. Werneth, in their first innings, ran up 47, and then Huddersfield tried their bands and totalled 19, 5 by Bamford, the first man, and 14 by Berry, the second. The remainder failed to add a single run.—Stockport must be able to put in the field a strong eleven, judging from Saturday's nerformance. The com- mittee had two engagements to meet, one at Altierley Edge and the other at Bowdon. At Alderley the total obtained was 268 to their opponents' 29, and at Bowdon 247 against their opponets 64.—At Oxford on Wednesday the Fresh- men's match concluded by Mr. Bastard's side being declared winners by three wickets. Score :—Mr. Page's side, 213 and 116; Mr. Bastard's side, 249 and 81 with three wickets to spare.

At an emergency lodge of Freemasons at the Town Hall, Yarmouth, on Thursday night, Prince Albert Victor, was passed to the second degree. The hearing of the charge preferred by Mr. Harrington, M.P., against Inspector Carr, of using unnecessary force in ejecting persons from Mallow railway station on the occa- sion of the recent visit of the Prince of Wales, was re- sumed on Wednesday, when the magistrates dismissed the case. MEnrarci OF Musuus.-oa*Fridav evening a meeting of the miners of St. Helens was held on the Market-equate to consider the questions of organisation, restricting the out. put, and assisting the Yorkshire miners, who are out on btike. Toe principal speaker was Mr, Thomas Glover, miners' agent. The following resolutions were unanimously passed :—" Teat we, the miners of St. Helens district, pledge ourselves to support the miners of Yorkshire, who are resisting. a ten per cent. reduction in their wages, by each man paying threepence per week; " and " We are of opinion Oat the great depression in the coal trade, and thi, frequent reduction of miners' wages are attribut.ble to over- production, and are mainly encouraged by unfair land lawe •trid the disorganisation in our ranks, and as a remedy wt would strongly urge upon the miners of this district the great necessity of a closer union."

div.head: SCANDALOUS CONDUCT OF A FRESCOT SURGEON. EXEMPLARY PUNISHMENT.
div.p: SCANDALOUS CONDUCT OF A FRESCOT SURGEON. EXEMPLARY PUNISHMENT.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Smith, Daniel Murray O'Hara, alias Owen Patrick O'Hara, alias William Law, ot Prescot, was placed in the dock and pleaded guilty to having, at Huyton, on the 26th Novena- , ber, and also at Sutton and Present, in October, 1884, • feloniously acted and professed to act under a false colour and pretence of the process of the County Court of Lanca- shire, holden at St. Helens; also to having, at Prescot and I West Derby, on December 10th, sent menacing letters to r Jane Amelia Griffith demanding without reasonable cause £2l, and on the 15th December in the same manner de- manded the sum of £42 ss. He was also charged with ob- . ; taining from Mrs. Griffiths £5 Ile. 61., and £lO 10s. from I Edward Lyon Evans. Mr. Heywood prosecuted, and Dr. • O'Feely appeared for the defence. I; Mr. Heywood said Vie prisoner bad pleaded guilty to ! several serious charges. It appeared Ott Mrs. Griffiths was • almost unknown to the prisoner, but he had met her once, just for a moment, two years ago, when he was acting as assistant to Dr. Wynne, at Kirkdale. At the end of last ; year the prisoner was sued by a firm in Brietol to recover a ; debt for drugs, and apparently the serving of that writ gave ; him an idea of practising this cruel fraud upon Mrs. • Griffiths, because it was then that he sent the first letter to her. Unfortunately, instead of putting this letter in the fire she replied to it, and further letters followed. At an • interview which the prisoner had with her, he stated that a . Mrs. Lewis and a Mr. Wynne, two persons known to her I before. but in a perfectly honourable manner, had brought an action against him at Bristol, intending to prove that he I had practised abortion upon Mrs. • Griffiths prior to her marriage. He induced her to believe that ; in order to protect her he must go to Eris- • tot and defend the action. In this way be ob- tained money from her. He went by the name of O'Hare, and pretended that O'Hara was the only man • who could keep the thing secret. He afterwards went through the form cf pretending to Mrs. Griffiths that he had been to Bristol, and in one of his letters he gave an account ! of the magnificent way in which he had defended the action. • He then presented to her a so-called attorney's bill, which be sa:d had been taxed and amounted to £4B. Prior to that I date the prisoner had got ten guineas from the lady's 1 brother. Having persuaded her that the proceedings were at an end, he commenced with a fresh letter, in which he practically said, "Although these proceedings are at an end, , I have in my possession documents which will prove this charge," and he persuaded her that unless she gave him money he would himself proclaim these atrocious charges. Having; got venous sums of money ont of her he called upon her, and at this time she had begun to suspect that a system of fraud was being practised upon her, because she had made inquiries and learned that Lewis was in Ireland, and that all about his being at Bristol was false. Mrs. Griffiths was afraid to tell the prisoner exactly that he had been getting money by false pretences, but she did say that she dis- believed him. He then went away in a huff, and wrote the letter of the Ilth February, which was the eubject of the principal indictment. In it he said, "Upon my reaching Edge-blil I found my excitement cooled down, and, as promise:4, I did not go to Liverpool, but wired to Bristol the following." Then ho pretended to have sent this telegram : She repudiates all. Charges me with fraud, and receiv- ing money under false pretences. Promised not to move until Weduaday, the 28,h inst. What shall I do ? Wire." then he alleged to hive received a reply as follows t— " Deserves no consideration, and shall get none. Don't in- terfere ; the case shall not be delayed one houi, Wire to 'ln. Collins, toy Liverpool agent, to call on you and get all documents." Then the priaoner went on to say that Mr,

Collins lead called upon him for the papers, which he had I refused. Mr. Collins had promised her until to-morrow. He (the prisoner) regretted her treatment bitterly, and of- fered to take the money by instalments. In case he got no message he would assuredly give up the papers. After read- ing this letter, the learned counsel said there was not a scin- tilla of ftmedation for any of these cluet charges, and the whole of the prisoner's statements were absolutely false. With reference to the other charne, of obtaining money under colour of a county court process, it seemed that the prisoner had a small debt owing to him by a Mrs. Fairhurst, and he went to the County Court and obtained a form to fill up. Then he went to her, and she being unable to read or write he told her it was a county court summons, and that unless she paid the money she would be sent to gaol The prisoner bad been convicted of a similar offence in Bel- fast in 1878, and his name was subsequently removed from the list of practising surgeons. fie (Mr Heywood) had in his hand a letter from the superintendent of police at Bel- fast stating that the prisoner was a notorious swindler, always obtaining money by different means —A sergeant of police at Belfaet was called, and icleatitied the prisoner as Patrick O'Hara.—Robert Dick, clerk to the prison at Bel- fast, proved that the prisoner was convicted and sentenced to twelve months' hard labour.—Dr. O'Feely : Was there anything peculiar in bis manner ?—Witness : During the first six months he pretended to be dumb and would not speak.—Dr. O'Feely said it was exceedingly diffi- cult to say anything in extenuation of the prisoner's offence. The prisoner had pleaded guilty, and had withdrawn all the charges against Mrs. Griffiths.—llis Lordship accepted the statement that the prisoner was a man of unquestionable ability, and had for 25years been a member of a noble and honourable pro- fession. How and why the prisoner departed from the path of probity he knew not. A more dastardly and abominable menace was never made. He (the learned judge) appreciated what had been said by the learned counsel for the defence, but it seemed to him that this charge was never withdrawn until the hand of the law was upon the prisoner, and until there was no possibility of escape. He did not know whether he was justified in the sentence he was about to pass, and it might be asked why he had not given the prisoner penal servitude for life. The sentence of the court was that the prisoner be kept in penal s.avitude for ten years.
liHE EXAMINER sit TITIMA Y. MAY 9. 1885

div.head: EARLESTOWN.
div.p: EARLESTOWN.

WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.—A meeting in connec- tion with the senior division of the Wesleyan Band of Hope Society was held in the Brunswick Wesleyan school, Cross- lane, on Thursday evening. There was a fur attendance, and Mr. J H. Graham presided. Several readings, circ, were given, and a very pleasant evening was spent. CONSERVATIVE MEETING.—The Central Association of the Conservative General Council for the Newton Divi- sion of South-West Lancashire, held a meeting in the magi- strates room at the Town Hall, Newton, on Thursday evening. There was a fair attendance of representatives, including Mr. M. B. Wesshead, Newton, who presided. The proceedings were not of a public character. DEATH OF MRS. MORRIS —The death of Mrs. Mary Morris, wife of Mr. Richard Morris, of the Sunbeam Inn, Wargrave Old-road, on Monday morning, occasioned much sorrow among a large circle of friends. Some three months ago, the deceased underwent an operation for a cancer in the breast, and for a time she seemed to be improving, but ether complications manifested themselves, and notwithstanding the diligent attentions of Dr. Fox, of Warrington, and Dr. Mouncey, of Earlestown, she expired on Monday at the age of 48 years, leaving eight children to mourn their loss. As the headquarters of the Earlestown Football Club, the Sun- beam Inn was well known, and Mrs. Morris manifested a keen interest in the comfort and success of the players, whom she familiarly termed "My lads." The remains of the deceased were interred in Wargrave Church on Wednes- day afternoon, and sea mark of respect and sympathy about 20 members of the Earlestown Football Club, with a large number of other friends, walked in procession with the cortege. The funeral service was performed by the Rev. Canon Whitley. On the coffin were three wreaths, one of which bad been forwarded from the members of the club. _ _ _

HATDOCK CONSEETATITES —A meeting of the Con. servatives of Ilaydock was held in the large room of the Wagon and Horses Hotel, on Tuesday evening, to consider the organisation of the Conservative party in the district relative to the new registration of voters, and to elect members of the Conservative Council of Newton Division of South-West Lancashire. There was a good attendance, and Mr. R. Bradshaw presided. Mr. Woodnorth, of Liver- pool, explained the provisions of the Franchise Bill and its privileges, after whic a the Chairman stated that the members of the Council woald be expected to look after the registration of voters. Mr. R. Bradshaw was appointed chairman pro. tem., Mr. Tho-nas Jackson and Mr. W. Bat- harry, vice-presidents, and Mr. Halton, secretary The following gentlemen were afterwards elected members of the Council :—Messrs. J. Helton, J. Cunliffe, E. Jenkins, J. Marsh, J. Tunstall, Rainford, T. Cunliff,., J. Jackson, T. Jackson, E. Naylor, A. Rimmer, W. Johnson, W. Stirrup, J. Abbott, W. Balhariy, J. Turton, R. Bradshaw, H. Ellison, G. Platts, H. Mayhew, W. Atherton, J. 0 wen, R. Whitnall, A. Litham, B. Lowe, C. Derbyshire, Dr. Beaman. E. Wiswell, and M. Cunliffe. The meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

Thu EARLESTOWN Gosrst Blirssrotr.—On Sunday special sermons were held in the Co-operative Hall, in con- nection with the Gospel Mission, the object being to reduce a debt on the harmonium. In the afternoon a service of song, entitled " The Lord's lilies," was splen- didly given by the choir, under the leader- ship of Mr. H. J. Darman. Mr. J. Bridge, of St. Helens, officiated as reader. In the evening the choir gave a service of song, entitled "The Good Shepherd," and Mr. Bridge again read the connective pieces. In appealing for liberality at the close of each service, Mr. Bridge, of St. Helens, said he was desired by the Gospel Mission Commit- tee to furnish them with a little information as to the object for which they were met together. As most of them would be aware, it was to reduce the debt still existing on the harmonium. In order to make the singing as corgregational as possible the committee felt it requieite to purchase a powerful instrument in November last, at a coat of £3O. Since then they had railed £2O, leaving a debt of £lO. The services were entirely free, and they had been obliged to resort to that special means of raising money to clear off the debt. It was hoped the friends would do their best to make the effort a success. A fair sum was realised at each ser- vice.

THE LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT FOOTBALL ORAL/MIME Cree.—This splendid trophy, won by the Earlestown Foot- ball Club, has at last found a resting place in Earlestown. It is a fine piece of workmanship, and the design is attrac- tive. It stands about two feet in height apart from the black ebony stand, of about nine inches. On the stand are three silver shields on which respectively are the inscrip- tions, " Bootle F.C. winners, 1883 ;'' " Everton F.C. win- ners, 1884 ;" and " Earlestown F.C. winners, 1885." On one side of the cup is an engraved representation of a foot- ball match, and on the obverse is a Liver bird, surrounded by a scroll on which are the words "Liverpool and District Football Challenge Cup." The cup is surmounted by a lid or cover, upon which is a solid silver representation of a footballer standing erect with his right foot on a hall. The model measures about five inches in length. The gold medals, one for each of the players composing the success- team, are correspondingly neat and of a suitable design. On one side is a Liver bird, and in four spaces are the letters " L.D.F.A.," meant for " Liverpool District Football Association." On the reverse side appears the inscription "Challenge Cup, 1885, Earlestown F.C. winners." Beneath is the name of every player of the Earlestown team—the name of each player being engraved on one of the medals. The cup and gold medals were publicly presented by his worship the Mayor of Liverpool to the representatives of the Earlestown Club on Monday evening. The presentation took place in the Liverpool Gymnasium after the annual sports in connection with that institution. The trophy and the medals were received by Mr. James Duxbury on behalf of the club, and they were subsequently conveyed to Earles- town, Neither the trophy nor medals have been publicly exhibited, it being the in!ention of the officials of the club to publicly present them at a gathering in the Viaduct Institute. Mr. Thomas Stone, of Newton, president, has kindly consented to distribute the medals. The cup and medals were conveyed to Mr. Stone's residence on Thurs- day, where they will remain until the preseptation. CONCERT AT NEWTON TOWN HALL —The annual con- cert in connection with the St. Peter's singing class. New- ton, was held in the Town Hall on Tuesday evening, and was a gratifying success. The assembly-room had been de- corated for the occasion by Mr. E. T. Evans, of Earlestown, and had a pleasing appearance. The platform was covered with red baize and white lace, while the windows were draped with white curtains. There was a crowded attend- ance. The clan 3, numbering about 50 members, sang" The hardy Norseman " in capital style, after which Mr. J. Bar- ber was encred for his rendering of "The midshipmite." He repeated the last verse. "Some day" was then sung by Miss Hewitt, and Mr. D. S. Williams, of Liverpool, a blind singer, gave " To .n Bowling." He possesses a fine tenor voice, and on being warmly recalled he excellently. ren- dered a concertina solo. Miss McCoy next sang "Children's voices" (with an invisible chorus), and in response to de- mands for an encore the last verse was again sung. Messrs. Leather and Evans were rewarded with enthusiastic ap- pl tales for their rendering of the duet "Sound out the trumpet." Miss Houghton efficiently accompanied on the pianoforte. " Where the bee sucks" was given by Miss A. Carr, who sang " The ivy green" as an encore. Mr. A. Hudson effectively rendered "Maud," and was encored ; Miss F. Kean, who sang "I have no home," being similarly rewarded. The first part of the pro- gramme then concluded with the part song " May- day. " by the class. The class afterwards gave "The stars are with the voyagers." Mr. F. Appleton, possessing a capital biritone voice, subsrqueetly sing " The little hero " with eff -et, and was loudly applauded. Miss S. Wheeler gave "Last night," and repetted the last portion as an en- core ; and Mr. D. S. Williams, who gave original " Prize selections" on the concertina,created unbounded enthusiasm. His selection was deservedly encored. The song "Dying embers " by Master W. Boardman had an "invisible chorus" in which Mr. F. Appleton, Mr. Hudson, Miss R tn- dell, and Miss Carr took part, and an encore was demanded. Messrs. Evans. Williams, and Leather were also recalled for their rendering of "The mouse-trap." Mr. W. Evans sang " True blue" and a humorous piece entitled "Where Pat came o'er the Wile," alter which Miss L. Turton Was re- called for her rendering of "By the sad sea waves." "Kit the cobbler " was given by Mr. W. Leather, to the accom- paniment of Miss Houghton ; the elms sang "Sir Knight, Sir Knight," and the progremme coneltded with the National Anthem,

MR. H. J. DURMAN'S CONCERT. The Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, was crowded to its utmost capacity on Monday evening, when Mr. 11. J. Darman (late organist of St. John's Church) gave a mis• c-Ilaneous concert. In every sense the gathering was a great success the chief feature of which was "Mr. Dar- man's string band" The hand was composed of about 15 local musicians, and far a first appearance made a most favourable impression on their hearers. Their selections were splendidly given, and the audience highly appreciated their efforts. The programme was opened with the "Over- ture to Samson "—a somewhat difficult piece for a new band. 'The performers, however, creditably acquitted therneelves, and were rewarded with enthusiastic applause. Mrs. Hunwick then sang "Lady of the Lea' with great feeling. Mr. H. McEleney, the bandmaster °lathe Viaduct Institute brass band, next gave a clarionet solo," The trum- pet march 'S (Jude). The piece was brilliantly executed, and he was warmly recalled. "The pilgrim of love" re- c-ived a good interpretation from Mr. J. Greenall, of Bryn. Mr. Greenall made his first appearance as an artiste in Earlestown, and be acquitted himself well. He possesses a tine tenor voice, both clear and strong. Miss Katie Williams, al St. Helens, prize winner at the Welsh National Eisteddfod at Liverpool, received a hearty welcome. The impressive and descriptive song, "The cuckoo on the birch-tree " created prolonged enthusiasm, and the young artiste was demonstratively encored. She responded with a pianoforte solo. Miss Lewis and Mrs. Hunwick nicely sang the duet " Friendship," after which Mr. B. F. McTear, son of Captain McTear, of St. Helens, give an oboe solo entitled " Fantasia," from Faust (Reynolds.) Mr. McTear is a musician, for, though his classical selection required con- siderable judgment and skill, his performance was really first class, and was highly appreciated. "The old cottage clock" was creditably sung by Miss Lewis, after which the band excellently rendered " Lift up your heads." After a short interval, the second part was opened with the March and chorus "Sing unto God "by the band. This was one of the best executed pieces of the evening, and wis well re- oeived. The pathetic song "I cannot mind my wheel, mother " was given by Mrs. Hunwick, and Mr. J. Greenall sang " Tont Bowling," after which Miss Lewis nicely gave Gounod'e "Serenade." A splendid clarionet performance by Mr. McEleney entitled "Reminiscences of Scotland" (Godfrey) created unbounded enthusiasm, and the perfor- mance was deservedly encored. Miss Katie Williams was also recalled for her brilliant rendering of " With the dawn," and as a response she repeated the last verse in Welsh. The next item on the programme was a sang " The desert " by Mr. H. J Darman. As Mr. Darman made his appearance, he was warmly wel- comed. He proceeded to explain that he was suffering from a severe cold, but the audience would take no denial. He then sang the piece in splendid style, and on being re- called, gave by request the amusing piece "The little scrub." " The elfin call " duet was effectively sung by Miss Lewis and Mrs Hunwick. Mr. Darman then thanked the audience for their presence that evening, and for their good wishes towards him. (Applause.) The band gave Mozart's " Gloria " from the 12th mass, after which the national anthem brought a very enjoyable concert to a close.
NEWTON COMMISSIONERS. HIONTHLY MEETING.

The monthly meeting of the Newton Improvement Corn• missioners was held at the Town Hall on Monday after• noon when there were present—Mr. W. F. Gooch (in the chair), Colonel George McCorgood tie, Messrs. T. J. Gilles- pie, J. Fairciough, T. Forster, B. B. Glover. J. W. Emmett, and T. Hunt ; Mr. J. E. Worsley (Jaw clerk), and Mr. R. Brierley (surveyor). The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed. THE COMBHSSIONBRS T. THB WARRINCITaIi GUARDIANS,

In alluding to the recent decision of the Judge of the Warrington County Court in the case of the Newton Com- missioners against the Warrington Board of Guardians, Dr. J. W. Watkins (medical officer of health) asked what he was to do in case of a serious outbreak of infection. They were in a very taculiar position now. The community would be divided into those who were unmistakeably paupers and those who might be temporarily pauperised. He would refer them to what he considered the insufficient provision at present existing with reference to the isolation of infectious diseases; and whether they would take up the question of making local provision. It Was a very costly arrangement and unsatisfactory one at present.—The Chair- man said the Commissioners had not considered the matter at all, and he thought it should previously be referred to the committee.—Mr. Worley thought that would be the beat thing to do.—Colonel McCorgeodale said the doctor could be assured that the points he had raised would not be lost sight of.—Mr. Worslay subsequently stated that the case wag duly entered in the Warrington County Court, and upon what he must describe as a purely technical point la decision was given against the Commissioners upon that particular case. The question WAS whether, under the cir- cumstances stated to the Judge, the Commissioners were entitled to recover from the Guardians the sum of £3O. The technical point which he bad mentioned was that which he had at first pointed out as that which the Commissioners had to face, and the Guardians took it up, and upon that point the judge decided that the Commissioners could not recover. The verdict was given for the Guardians (the defendants) and that was how the matter stool—The Chairman again expressed the opinion that the question should be referred to the committee.—Dr. Watkins pointed out that a family like Harria's might be a whole fortnight in waiting for the decision of the Guardians. Whatever the Newton Relief Committee might do must be confirmed by the Guardians, who only held fortnightly meetings.—The Chairman: The committee have power to deal with these cases ?—Dr. Watkins: No; you have lost it on these tech- nical grounds. Mr. Fairclough said he thought it would be sufficient if they got an order from the relieving officer. The Chairman said if the local Relief Committee decided that any case was a proper pauper case the reference of their proceedings to the Board of Guardi ens was a mere formality.—Dr. Watkins said he could not force any man to be a pauper. That would sim- ply be Intolerable; but a man was a pauper when he ap- plied for assistance.—Colonel McCorquodale suggested that until they had proper arrangements with the Board of Guardians Dr. Watkins be instructed to get relief orders from the relievieg officer.—Dr. Watkins said it was not within his province to de th it. Though he might go to a patient as medical officer, he could not compulsorily pan- periee the people.—The Chairman: Whose duty is it ?—Dr. Watkins: No one can pauperise a man.-Colonel McCorquo- dale said no doubt suitable arrangements would be made, and Dr. Watkins might use his own discretion in the meantime —The Chairman remarked that they seemed to be in a very unsatisfactory position; and Mr. Gillespie asked if any harm was done if the Board applied to the Guardians for information as to how they were to proceed in similar cases in the future ?—The Chairman thought it would be a good thing to have a meeting between the Guardians and the Commissioners in reference to the question.—Colonel Mc- Corquodale subsequently moved that the Law-Clerk be in- structed to see Mr. Sutton, as clerk to the Guardians, if suitable arrangements could be made for the present —Mr. Gillespie seconded the motion.—Mr. Glover meved as an amendment that the question be referred to the Sanitary Committee.—Mr. Forster seconded the amendment, which was carried.

RIORWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTER. The Highways, Public Works, and sanitary Committee held a meeting oil the 20th April. Dr. Watkins stated that he desired to keep before the committee that part of his annual report recommending the provision of cottage hos- pital for the treating of infectious diseases in the district After some discussion the subject was postponed. A letter was read from Mr. Beasley, architect, Earlestewn, stating that he was laving out Mr. Houghton's land for building purposes, and he wished to know if Mr. Houghton gave a portion of land for footpath whether they would agree to make and pave the same. It was ordered that Mr. Beesley be informed the Commissioners agree to curb the footpath, and that the cost of flaggisg and paving the same be borne equally by the Commiraioners and the lessees of the adjoin- log land lying south of the Manchester and Liverpool rail- way, these terms to extend only to the north of the said railway, on Mr. Legh agreeing to the same respecting his land which abuts upon Wargrave-road.—Tho Surveyor sub- mitted a draft of his scheme for dealing with the &maga below the canal at Earlestown (west) outlet. It was ordered that the same be approved with the application of Hanson'a automatic mixing machine, and that the surveyor wait upon Mr. Worthington with his plans as soon as possible. The surveyor having certified the SIM of 1100 due to Mr. J Pennington on big eewer, &c., contract, and to Mr. J. Roth- well the sum of £2OO on his contract for cemetery build- ings. Cheques for these amounts were ordeted to be drawn. —The following building plans were submitted and ap- proved :—Two houses in Market-street for Mr. N. Slinn. three houses in Wargrave-road for Messrs. G. Walton, J White, and J. Moos; also alterations of privies and yards in Cebden-square for Mr. H. Houghton. Plans for ten cot- tages in Gas-street for Meeers. Walton & Co. were put back for arrangements for a strip of land for proposed siding to gasworke.—The minutes were passed.
GAS AND WATER.

The Gas and Water Committee held a meeting on the 20th nit It was ordered that Mr. Brierlev wait upon Messrs. Walton rt; Co., Gas-street, to ascertain upon what terms they would grant a strip of land adjoining the street for the proposed siding to the gasworks, according to plan submitted by him to this committee. It was resolved that , the necessity for a bond in Mr. Dale's contract for tar and ammonlacal water be not enforced. The carbonizing ac- count for the past month gave fuel used 196 tons cwt. ; gas made 1,956,000 cubic feet, averaging 9,974 feet per ton of fuel used. Mr. P. Ctitchley attended to make applica- tion for a reduction in the water charge for Earlestown bowling green, when he was informed tnat the committee would he willing to reconsider the charges after next season. —The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

At a meeting of the Finance Committee on the 20•1 h April, the estimates for the rates to be laid in May were ordered to be prepared. Accounts amounting to £734 105 31 were passed for payment.—The rninutcs were passed. • SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. • •

At a meeting of the School Attendance Committee on the 20th April, Mr. Ball having read his report, was questioned upon several absentees, nod upon his explanations it was resolved that the school teachers of the district be asked to furnish a fortnightly return of absentees to Mr. Ball, and that he submit the name to each meeting of the Committee with the roeult of his itlairies written thereon; the school registers (copy) kept by Mr. Ball to be suspended until further orders. It was resolved that an additional XlO be added to Mr. Ball's salary for keening a copy of the school registers for the year just ended.—The follcwirg fipres
were stated to be from the records of the school registers ending March quarter:
No. on Average Per Schools. books. attendance. centsge. St. Peter's Gas-street Wargrave Farlest'on District Infants 182 155 801 Wesleyan Roman Catholic Vulcan 154 75 48f Saekey Various
Totals — 2178 1540

Corresponding quarter last year 2279 1787 78 2-5 The falling off ha the attendance was caused by an epidemic of scarlet fever and measles, which had prevailed since August last.—Mr. Worsley subsequently said that at a previous meeting he was directed to write a letter to the Education Department respecting the non-attendance of children at school. He had written stating that during the past year there had been serious oatbreaks of fever and measles, which were prevalent daring the last few months of 1884. He had been requested to write to the Education Department stating that the average attendance at the schools had been affected to a very considerable extent. The managers of the schools wished that to be laid before the Department, and to have pointed out to them the great disadvantage they had to labour under. They hoped the circumstances would be taken into account at the examina- tions. He (Mr. Worsley) had received a reply horn the Education Department to the effect that the statement had been received, and they would instruct their inspectors to bear the statements in mind at the next examinations. RATES FOR THE ENSUING YEAR% Mr Glover proposed, in accordance with the recommen- dations of a special meeting of the Finance Committee, that for the year ending 25th March, 1886, the various rates be as follows:—General improvement rate (including cemetery), Is Id in the £ ; gis rate, 24 in the £ ; water rate, 24 in the £; and water rate for Park-side sub-district, 3.1 in the £. It was explained that the new cemetery had caused an addition of 44 to the gene:al improvement rate; otherwise the rates were same as last year.—Mr. J. W. Em- mett seconded the motion, which was passed. THE COSTS OF THE RECENT ACTION. Mr. Worsley said that he might supplement what he had previously stated with respect to the case against the Guar- diane, that the bill of costs had been sent in ; and it amounted to £66. It had, however, been taxed down to £29 2s. (A laugh). THE ALLEGED ENCLOSURE OF A PUBLIC FOOTPATH. The Law Clerk said lee was instructed at the last meet- ing to write to Mr. Pardey respectiag the road across the Mesnes. He bad written a letter stating that he was in- structed by the Commissioners to write respecting the ob- struction of an ancient footpath across the Mesnes by the erection of a wooden fence by the Football Club. The foot- path bad been used for a great number of years, and it was shown on the ordnance map for the district as a public foot- path. He was instructed to ask for the removal of the obstruction and thus throw the footpath open to the public. —Mr. Emmett : On the ordnance map is it ? That is very important.—Mr. Worsley added that it was. Mr. Pardey had replied that the enclosure did not stop up or interfere with any public footpath. The estate plan which dated back half a century, showed the footpaths very clearly, and would he (Mr. Pardey) thought, satisfy them there was no ancient footpath through the land which had been fenced off. Mr. Worsley ad led that he had called upon Mr. Pardey and had seen the estate plan, which did not show any footpath.—ln reply to Mr. Emmett, the Law Clerk said the estate plan was 1840 something.—Mr. Glover said a footpath was not required to be used for 40 years to become a right to the public. Mr. Pardey producing a plan 50 years old did not affect that focapath.—Mr. Gillespie: The fact of it being marked en the ordnance map is very signific int.—Colonel McCorquodale: What is the date of the ordnance map?— Mr. Worsley: 1843 and 1845.—Mr. Emmett: Well, that is 40 years the road has been open, and it does appear by that that the public have a right to claim that the road shall be open.—The Chairman thought the public had a perfect right to claim it as a public footway.—Mr. Glover asked what was the result of the interview 'with Mr. Pardey ? Mr. Worsley said Mr. Pardey seemed to base everything on the fact that the footpath was not shown on his plans, but he (Mr. Worsley) pointed out that the footpath was shown on the ordnance maps. Mr. Pardey replied that people had always been stopped, and boards had been put up prohibit- ing people using the footpath.--Mr. Glover asked if Mr. Pardey had been informed that the Board could maintain their right by evidence, and that in the interests of the ratepavere they meant to keep the path open.--alr. Wors- ley: Not in so many words, but he knew I was going to bring it before you to take your instructions.—The Chair- man: Has the Board proper authority to take action in the matter.—Colonel McCorquodale asked what number of years was required to make the footpath public P—Mr.Fairclough : Twenty-one yearta—Mr. Gillespie never remembered the gate having been kept locked, and he had never been pre- vented going through it.—Mr. Emmett observed that there was a wicket gate which proved it had been a public foot- path.—Mr. Brierley: Not now, but there has been one.— The Chairman: I have been over that road, and never had any interference. —The Chairman thought the matter had better be referred to the Highway rtad Public Works Com- mittee, and Mr. Glover moved a motion to that effect—Mr. Gillespie seconded the motion.—Mr. Fairclough subse- quently remarked that the Mesnes had been pretty well used by the public, and be felt rather sore on the footpath business. People went through gates and made short "cots" across fields fora.bout two years and then claimed the right.a road.—Mr. Gillespie: Then you are a prejudiced party P—Mr. Fairclough : Yes, I don't like people to go across a field and then claim P.—lt was decided to refer the matter to the com- mittee.

THE NEW CEMETERY. The Law Clerk said he had been asked to send for the use of the Bishop's Secretary plans showing the divisions and information as to the boundaries between the conse- crated and unconsecrated portions of the new cemetery. He also wanted to know the approximate date the ground would be ready for consecratioa.—Mr. Gillespie observed that Mr. Brierley could give the information.—The Chairman said there were no immediate requirements for the ground.—Mr. Brierley added that there had been no applications.—Col. McCorquodale : There is still room in the other church- yards.—The Chairman would. not like things to be hurried. —Mr. Glover said it was clearly understood that the chapel was not to be consecrated. He should not like to fled them- selves in a position that the Bishop had consecrated the building—The Chairman: That is the intention, I bAteve. —Mr. Glover said then they as Nocconforrnists would call on that Board to erect two different buildings.—Mr. Gilles- pie : You would not know whether it was consecrated or not.—The matter then dropped.

IMPROVEMENTS AT WARGRATE. Mr. Brierley said he had served notices on the owners of property abutting on Wargrave-road, calling upon them to pave and sewer the said road. He had received a letter from Mr. Pardey, dated the 4th May, in which he said that the road referred to was a public highway and that the sewering and paving Was not a charge which could be made on the owners of the abutting land.—The Chairman asked if the road had ever been repaired by the township, and Mr. Brierley replied that it had net —The Chairman thought the matter was one for the Law Clerk to deal with. —Mr. Glover thought the proper course was to allow the notice to expire and then proceed with the work. If the owners of land refused to pay proceedings could be taken to recover the amounts due.—The Chairman said that was so —The subject then dropped. This was the principal business.

MARRIAGE OF LORD RIPON'S ELDEST SON.—The mar- riage of Earl de Grey, eldest son of the Marquis of Ripon, with Constance Gladys, Countess of Lonsdale, widow of the late Earl of Lonsdale, was solemnised on Thursday fore- noon at the Church of St. Martin's-in-the-Fields, London, by the vicar, the Rev. Mr. Humphrey& The wedding Wag strictly private. TETE CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE FOR ST. HELENS.— The central committee of the St. Helens Conservative Reg- istration Association held a meeting on Monday night to select a gentleman to contest the borough at the next election in the Conservative interest. There was a good attendance, and Major Windus presided. Mr. H. Seton- Karr,.barrister of Kippilaw, Roxburghshire, Mr. H. Baxter, J.P., of St. Helens, and Mr. Thomas Swift, barrister, Liver- pool and St. Helens, bad each been invited to state whether in the event of being selected as the Conservative candidate he would be willing to come forward. Replies were read from those gentlemen. Mr. Seton-KarK expressed his wil- lingness to accept the offer of the assodiation, but Mr. Hex. ter and Mr. Swift declined the honour, the first-named because of the unsatisfactory stab of his health, and the latter on account of pressure of professional duties. A !notion was subsequently unanimously pissed that Mr. Seton-Krrr be invited to meet the Central Committee with the view of his being adopted as the Conservative c indi- date.

FANCY FAIR AT Strrrox.—Ou Tuesday afternoon a fancy fair was opened in the new girls' school connected with St. Anne's Retreat of the Passionist Fathers, Sutton, St. Helens, by the Mayor of St. Helens (Alderman Cook), who, in performing the ceremony, said that whatever differences of oninion they might hare on religious aubjects, he was sure they could have none as. to the importtnce of the education of the people. (Applause ) They hnew that the Catholic church always considered that, along with secular: education, the religious element shoull be com- bined, and in consistency with hose principles they ob- served in those buildings what liberal provision had been made for the education of the peeple in that neighbourhood of the borough of St. Ilelexa.
