CONSECRATION OF ST. JOHN'S CHURCH, WALTON. The new church which has been erected at Walton by Sir Gilbert Greenall, was consecrated OR Thursday by Dr. Selig's, the Lord Bishop of Chester. The church, which is a hanasome and substantial structure, is situated in the midst of a burial ground of considerable size near to Walton village, and its tall tower forms a conspicuous feature of the landscape for some distance round. The style of the church is decorated Gothic. It is mciform in shape, the nave, including the tower, being 78 feet long and 21 feet 6 inches wide, and the chancel 37 feet long and 20 feet wide. The interior of the church presents a very tine appearance, hav- ing been richly and chastely finished. The roofs through- out are of oak, the nave and chancel having a " wagon- shaped " ceiling, beautifully illuminated with ecclesiastical designs and symbols. Eight panels at the extreme east end of the chancel ceiling are elaborately painted with angels holding scrolls containing the ten commandments, and around each angel is another scroll with the words " Lord have mercy on us, and incline our hearts to keep this law." There are several stained glass windows represent- ing scriptural incidents, and one of these windows, the westernmost on the south side of the nave, commemorates the dedication. The central compartment of the tracery con- tains the arms and crest of Sir Gilbert Greenall. In the floral ornament et side panels of tracery are entwined scrolls with the motto "Alta Pete." The quarries in the lower part of the window bear on a small scroll the motto as above and the monograms G. G. and S. G., the initials of Sir Gil- bert and Lady Greenall On a band through the three lights is the dedicatory inscription, "To the glory of God and in honour of St. John the Evanaelist, this church was erected and endowed by Sir Gilbert Greenall, baronet, A.D., MDCCC LXXXII." The reredos is of oak. In the centre• panel is represented the Saviour on the cross with the vir- gin mother on the left hand, and Joseph of Arimatbosi on the light. In the next panels are the figures of a Roman centurion, and of Mary Magdalene. The four panels forming the wings of the reredos contain the figures of the four evangelists. the weather on Thursday was not altogether propitious to a celebration of this kind, but not- I withstanding this there was a very large gather- ing. every seat in the church being completely filled. In addition to a considerable number of the local gentry, there were also many prominent inhabi- tants of Warrington present. Amongst the clergy who were in attendance were :—The Lord Bishop of Chester • Arch- deacon Darby ; Rev. Canon Greenall; the Rev. Leizester J. T. Darwall, incumbent of the new church; the Rev. S. Wilkinson, St. Paul's, Warrington; the Rev. Thos. Whitley, Dareebury ; the Rev. C. C. Ward, Newton-le-Willows; the Rev. W. B. Pratt, Daresbury; the Rev. E. Marsden ; the Rev W. H. Price, Oxford; the Rev. T. F. Tofts, St. Thotne 's, Stockton Heath ; the Rev. H. B. Blogg, Frodsharn ; the Rev. R. T. Whittington, Orsett, Essex; the Rev. F. Slater; and the Rev. E. Cr E. Carleton. The service was taken part in by the Rev. L. J. T. Darwall, the Rev. T. J.Whitley, and the Rev. T. &Toff. The Bishop took for his text the words, " Now unto Him that is able to do exceeding, abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us. Unto Him be glory in the Church, by Christ Jesus, throughout all ages, world with- out end. Amen." (Ephezians iii., 20, 21.) In the course of his sermon, his Lordship said that they were met that day to consecrate and to ask a blessing upon the new church—a very noble new church—with its new appliances, and everything which was useful and beautiful. The work was all well done, and was a labour of love, and a free offer- ing of the heart. He was sure that it was the prayer of all that day that the church would be abundantly blessed, and that the work of God would prosper them. Further than that, they were asking a blessing on the begin. Ding of a new stage of work. That new church was to be a new source and centre of radia- tioo, of light, and wartntb, and diffusion for the district in which it was placed. They enjoined in their prayers that it might be so blessed, and also prayed that blessings might be bestowed on the new minister who was just beginning the work of his new parish, and that he might be strengthened with might to declare his Master's will, and bring it horns to his people's hearts. They also prayed that his life might be kept pure, and that he might ke devoted to the work entrusted to him, and that he might have strength to prove himself a faithful minister ef the kingdom of righteousness. And further still, they were engaged in a work which would be of a pleasing character and spirit, and which would stimulate life in that neigh- bourhood, and strengthen its progress. However rapid the changes which the growth of population and the growth of manufacture might be in these central counties. he thought they must all realise that church work in its character was as distinctly missionary as that in the ancient churches. In new churches there was a departure from old associations, and old h tbits were abandoned altogether; and in the new state of things they required new lines and new methods to work upon. New towns sprang up, and in some of them there was no reason to look at the ancient state of things as being inadequ; ti Tnat particular parish, and that particular church, might be an exception to the rule. Every new church required appliances, and entered on a new system, eschewing the old customs which were good enough for their forefathers, and good enough for those who never thought whether they were good enough for the mg- vice of God. New churches required new working, new !sermons, and new things. Ministers and people would not content themselves with old ideas, but were adopting a new method. His Lordship hoped the work would go on with more grace, and that the work would be more eernest, more intelligent and sympathetic, and they should not be satis- fied until they had made the house of God beautiful and a place worthy of His service. Might that church be dm beacon of missionary light and example to perfect the love of God's service, and the good work which always accom- panies it. Further still, they knew by experience what good their parish chui ches had been to many for genera- tions: they were the places where their forefathers were married, and where many of them were christened and con- firmed for generations. Sa might that new church become the home of the soul like the ancient churches had been, having new management, and new armour for the service, and might it be a new stage of progress in defence of Ged's service. His Lorishio trusted that the work which had been begun that day would have God's blessing, and that it might be a substantial stage in the advancement of the glory which shall be on the church through Jesus Christ.— A large party was, after the service, entertained to luncheon by Sir Gilbert Greenall.

He had had very close relations with Mr. Walker for a long period, but never once had anything occurred that could reduce his respect for Mr. Walker in the slightest possible degree. ! Eighteen years ago last February he (the speaker) became editor of the Blackburn Times, on a change of proprietor- ship, and he found Mr. Walker at the office. Mr. Ernest King, the former proprietor of the paper, had discovered latent in Mr. Walker the literary gift, and hid taken him ' I from the office of a mill. Mr. Walker began life, as it was well that all lads should begin, on a comparatively low rung of the laid...yeas a clerk. He successively became junior ; reporter and chief reporter, and front that rose to the pO5l- ; lion of sun-editor and manager. and to that of literary con- tributor to the Preston Guardian and Blackburn Times.ll Twelve months ago he was drafted to another corner of the! county, and became editor of the Warrington Examiner, and he was now leaving some of them in the lurch—as it was always expected he would do—(laughter)—by developing into a newspaper proprietor. (Loud ap- plause.) They all rejoiced in the exhibition of enterprise by Mr. Walker, and wislascl for him a complete realisation of his wishes. Mr. Walker was the son of a Blackburn man—Mr. Edward Walker—who was a staunch defender of the rights of his class, independent in thought, and thoroughly upright in conduct. Mr. John Walker was ' a chip of the old block. Mr. Walker had not limited his services to his professional duties—be had been to the fore in almost everything that had been going on in the town during a long series of years. As a writer in the dialect, he , had published sketches, both on political and non-politicel I subjects, that for their point, shrewdness, and native wit were well worthy to rank with similar writinge of Edwin Waugh and Ben. Brierley. He had also written poetry of a high class, while his contributions to the local pantomime always contained a great deal of wit and a larger proportion of good puns than was usual in such matter. (Laughter.) , Mr. Walker bad great ability as a public speaker and de- hater. Not only had he done great Services On the platform,l but he took a leading position in the Blackburn Parlia- mentary Debating Society, and in that arena inspired the confidence of his political friends and the respect of his political opponents. Tbe word "Reformer" would represent as truly as any single word could do Mr. Walker's position not only in regard to political but in regard to social affairs. He had been characterised by thoroughness in his opinions, and he never flinched from upholding his principles. It was to be expected from Mr. Walker that he would have little tournies with the parsons when he got upon the School Board—(laughter)—as they was not very much harmony of thinking between a man of Mr. Walksr's views on one side, and the Rev. Father Maglione, for instance, on the other ; and they-need not wonder that the Rev. H. Wescce did not see eye to eye with Mr. Walker. (Renewed laugh- ter.) On all occasions Mr. Walker had advocated the rights of the people and self-government, against monopoly and sectarian ascendancy. He (the speaker) was sure that in IVarrington Mr. Walker would prove a great acquisition to the Press, the Liberal party, and the great public, which a local paper should always aim to serve. He had great pleasure in proposing "Good health, success, and long life to Mr. Walker and his family." (Loud applause.) Mr. JAMES GREEN endorsed what Mr. Abram had said, and added that be believed the Parliamentary Debating Society was broken up because it was found that they had too great a man in the person of Mr. Walker at the head of the Liberal party. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. L S. WAteestety observed that times of parting led them to look back to times of meeting, and, recalling the time when Mr. Walker first made an impression npon him a quarter of a century ago at a class in the old Mechanics' Institution, he could remember that be was then struck with his distinct individuality. He had always felt that Mr. Walker was a gentleman watchful for opportunities, with resolution to Seize and make the moat of them when they arose. (Applause.) Mr. JAMES KENYON observed that there were present re- presentatives of all shades of Liberal thought from all parts of Blackburn, 'end it was a great compliment to Mr. Walker that there were round that board men occupying foremost places in the Liberal party. Councillor Beads,J.P., chair- man of the Liberal Executive of the borough, was unable to attend owing to illness, but he was the bearer of a written message from him, which was as fellows :—" Cobden Villa, Blackburn, May 4th, 1885. My dear sir,—lf I could have been present at the complimentary dinner to Mr. John Walker this evening, I should have hart great pleasure in expressing the high esteem in which I have held him since I first met him in public life. I have found him truly loyal to advanced Liberal principles, when they were less popular than now. His pen, ever ready both in poetry and prose, has been effectively used for the good ef the Liberal party; whilst his platform addressee—always pleasant to listen to —havebeen marked by clearness, vigour., and convincing power. lam sorry we are losing him. Blackburn can ill afford to part with such men —especially Blackburn Liberalism. I wish him—whet I think he will have if health permits—a prosperous future. Warrington will have in Mr. Walker a man in whom the Liberal party there may repose the greatest confidence.—Hopine you will have a successful gathering this evening, lam, dear sir, very truly yours,JAmes BEADS." (Applause.) During the last few days dozens of men had to him expressed themselves in very warm terms in regard to Mr. Walker, knowing well the work he bad done on their behalf. Mr. Walker had excelled more than anything else in championing the rights of the people, es- pecially the poorer sections of the people, and no men round that board had more affectionate feelings towards him than had hundreds outside that roam. A man who lived in War- rington had assured him that Mr. Walker would there find many congenial spirits, and he (the speaker) hoped that he would succeed in his new sphere of life. (Applause.) The VICE-CHAIRMAN, after declaring that none would miss Mr. Walker more than he would, read a letter he had received from the Rev. John Johnston, pastor of the Mon- tague-street Congregational Church, in which he said :—" I exceedingly regret that, owing to a prior engagement, I am not able to be present this evening atthe dinner given by way of' farewell' to Mr. John Walker, of the Times. Mr. Walker is a gentleman f, r whom I entertain the very highest esteem, and it would have been a real pleasure to me to have taken part in this meeting held in his honour, even though the pleasure could not fail to be mingled with regret that the meeting was called te bid our friend Good- bye.' It may seem to some exaggerated language to use, yet I use it sincerely when I say that I do not know another men in Blackburn who, in his own particular sphere of pub. lic action, will be more keenly missed. Always honest, courteoue, fair, and charitable, the staunch friend of the poor, and tbelearless champion of the people's liberties, Mr. Walker has done a wore in Blackburn that no other Black- burnian whom ha leaves behind him has surpassed, or per- haps even E 0 much as equalled. His work upon the School Board alone in exposing and opposing the nefarious designs of sectarian bigote, and tierce political partisans who would sacrifice the best interests of the community for the sake of their particular Church and Party, and have been guilty of trickery that even eon-religious folks would hesitate to adopt, has teid all fair-minded and earnest educationalists under the deepest obligation " (Loud applause.) div.p: Covetous Tinnier—At Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday two young men, named William Griffiths and William Parkes, were convicted of stealing a hen and twelve duck's eggs, the property of James Rowles, labourer, Rixton. On &unity, the 26:4 ult , Rowles saw the hen sitting on the eggs in a stable attached ti his house, and shortly afterwards miFsed them. Information was given to the police, and prisoners, who had been seen loitering near the premises, were found with the hen and eggs in their possession. They were fined 408 and costa each, or go to prison for a month in default of payment. • EXTRAORDINARY ARREST OF A CONSTARLB.—An amus- ing incident, though at the same time one to be much re- gretted, occurred during the May Day festivities at Knuts• ford, where a member of the. Warrington borough police force, Constaffe Evans, was the subject of a gross mistake on ths part of the local police. It appears that Mr. Evans had obtain6d a holiday from his " Mr. Hunt, which he decided to spend at Knutsford, there to witness the first of May celebrations which have become so popular. Dur- ing the afternoon, a Kuutsford policeman took into custody a man who had rendered himself amenable to the law, and, as he appeared to be in need of assistance, Constable Evans, with a true policeman's inatinct, went te render it. The effr of help was, however, misinterpreted, and Evans soon found Women transformed from an officer of the law to a prisoner. Against this he very naturally protested, but was taken to ths police office, where he soon convinced the mis- taken officials that they had been doing a foolish thing. He was, of course, at Once Set at liberty, and reparation in the shine of apologies was readily made. It is said that the , Warrington conetable produced sufficient proof to set bia identity and position be, oncl doubt before he was taken to the police station, and if that be so, it is strange that he should hive been subjected to an indignity after endeavour- ing to do a kind action to his comrades in the force. The Knutsford polioemen seem to have mistaken him at first for some one connected with the perssn who had been mis- conducting himself. The cc-urrence created some amuse- tn,nt on becoming known in Warrington and much Merrily sympathy was displayed to Constable Evans, who has been in the borough force since 1890, and bears a cbaracterabove suspicion. The affair leads to a surmise that is worth men- tioning. Had not Constable Evans been able to bring in- disputable proof that he was a constable, what might have been the end of the mattsr ? It is not too rash a supposi- tion to say that it is quite possible that he might have had to malts an appew aces b,fore the magistrates, and with not very pleasant results. Mistakes, it is evident, will happen in the best regulated po' ice force,

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Snow again fell in North Staffordshire on Friday morn- ing, and the weather continues to be extremely cold. It is notified in Friday night's Gazette that the Queen %ill hold a drawing-room at Buckingham Palace OH Wed- nesday next. The publication of General Gordon's diary has been en- trusted to Mr. Egmont Hake, a cousin of the late distin- guished officer.
- Professor Huxley, deferring to the advice of his friends, is about to give himself a 'long period of rest from his arduous intellectull labour.

Mr. John Morley has consented to bEcome the president of the London and County L beral Union, in succession to Sir John Lubbock, who is about to resign. Mr. Thomas Burt, M.P., president of the National Asso- c'ation of Miners, his, in the name of the Association, is- sued an urgent appeal for help for the miners on strike in the Barnsley distric..
THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN. DEFEAIS OF THE MAHDPS FORCES.

DONGOLA, FRlDAY.—Reports continue to be received of defeats sustained by the M.ihdi's forces from Kordofan in- surgents and the garrison of Senaar. In the former case the Mandites sustained heavy loss, while in the fighting with the Senaar garrison their guns were captured. The remnant of the Mandi's forces retreated to Abu Haraz, and sent a request for reinforcements to the Mandi, who replied that he had none available. The Malidi is stated to be at Om- demean with a few troops. _ THE CANADIAN REVOLT.

OTTAWA, FRIDAY.—The steamer Northcote, which has hitherto been employed in the transport of supplies, has been converted into a gunboat, and will co-operate with the troops in the attack upon Riel, for which all the necessary preparations have been made. All the Indians west of Battleford are in war paint. There are numerous bands of hostile Indians in the region round Edmonton. Big Bear has taken the wives and children of several settlers prisoners.

THE PRO .'OSED ARBITRATION. BRUSSRLS, FRIDAY AFrEntrom.— The Independen-e Beige states that the Russian Government believes arbitra- tion will have no practical results, and that it will be abandoned in favour of a direct Anglo-Russian understand- ing on the whole Central Asian question. COPE:TAGER, FRlDAY.—Despite denials, it is certain that the King of Denmark will accept the office of arbitrator.
LORD DUFFERIN'S VIEW OF THE SI fUATION.

The Exchange Company telegraphs that it is able to state en excellent authority that there is no foundation for the report that Lord Dufferin has offered his resignation as Viceroy of India. The Central News is enabled to state that his Lordship suggested that an arrangement should be made with Russia after the first conference at Rawul Plod', when the Ameer expressed his disinclination to allow British troops to enter Afghinistan. The incident at Penjdeh, which occurred later, did not cause his Lordship to, alter his views In this respect, and he continues to advocate a compromise with Russia in respect to the disputed frontier lino, provided that the question arising out of General Komaroff's conduct could be arranged in a manner which would satisfy British honour.

THE ARBITRATION CONVENTION. The Central News has reason ta believe that the prelimi- nary convention for referring the Anglo-Russi in dispute respecting the interpretation of the covenant of March 17th to athitration. was signed by the representatives of both dis- putants at the Foreign Office on Thursday. A copy of the Convention is now on its way to Sr. Petersburg. ,

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
The House met at four o'clock.

TILE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN. Earl MOBLEY, replying to Earl Longford, said there were twenty-four or twenty-five thousand troops in the Soudan. Supplies of food and clothing were superabundant for Wady Haifa, and were forwarded rapidly.—Lord BURY inquired whether there had been want of boots at certain stations.—Earl MORLEY re- plied that no serious complaint had reached bim.—The Duke of CAMBRIDGE said that in no previous campaign had com- missariat been mere complete. The House shortly afterwards adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock.

THE VOTE OF CREDIT.—Sir S. NORTHCOTR, on behalf of Lord G. Hamilton, gave notice that, on Monday, he should move on the second reading of the Consolidated Fund Bill, a resolution to the effect that the House, having shown its readiness to grant such supplies as might be required for the defence of the Empire, before proceeding with it, is entitled , to receive from the Government full and adequate informa- tion as to the policy for which the money in the recent Vote of Credit is to be applied. THE FIGHTING IN THE SOI7DAN. Lord HARTINGTQN, replying to Mr. Morley and others, said he had nothing to add to the information given yesterday es to the engage- ment at Dakhdul. It did not appear thet the action of Gen. Graham was inconsistent with the statement made when the Vote of Credit WAS laid en the table. General Graham was bound to take steps to protect the Railway, and be thought General Graham perfectly justified in the measures taken to disperse the hostile tribes. ORDER OP FIISINICSS.—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Sir Stafford Northcote, said he proposed that the Houre should continue its sittings up to the Thursday before Whit Sun- day. Oa the Friday there would be the morning sitting, and then the House would adjourn until Thursday the week following, for Whitsuu holidays. On Thursday next the House should propose a resolution to make provision ter the Princess Beatrice on her marriage. THE SEATS BILL—The Redistribution Bill was coned- dared as amended.—Tbe discussion was resumed on an amendment moved by T. P. O'Consote to alter the bound- aries of the Exchange Ward, Liverpool, for the purpose of concentra ing Irish voters.—The amendment on a divi- sion was rejec'ed by 224 to 32.—The setting out of the various divisions of Southwark, Tower Hamlets,. and Westminster were agreed to.—Mr. Sarrom proposed that, instead of compass names of the four divisions for Dublin, they should be named College Green, Dublin Har- bour, Doonybrook, and St. Patrick's.—This was agreed to. —Mr. SLAGG proposed to change the name of one of the divisions of South .Eat Lancashire frcm Farnworth-cum- Radcliffe to Radcliffe-cum-Farnwortir—Mr. A. The Japanese village, which for some months has been eetab- fished at Albert Gate, Hyde Park, Lsndon, and which con- sisted of five streets of houses and shops constructed and. people i by Japanese, was destroyed by fire on Friday night. The conflagration raged from end to end of the line of build- ings, and the fire engines were engaged for eeveral hours in• attempting to snlidue the flames. As far as can be ascer- tained, no lives have been lost. ' Xoldiere from tha Knights- bridge Barracks rendered valuable assistance to the fire brigade and theoolice. The damage is estimated at £30,000.. ARCHDEACON BARDSLEY'S VISITA- TION AT WARRINGTON. On Wednesday the Yen. J W. Bardsley, Archdeacon of Warrington, visited the Parish Church, Warrington, for the perpoee of admitting the churchwardens and suleanien of the various churches in the town and district. In the course of his address he said that in a few instances it did not ap• pear that any provision was made for the safe-keeping of deeds and papers. In one case, and that one of their largest and most impertant parishes, it was reported to him, he was sorry to add, that "it was not known what had become of their deeds and papers." It was moth to be wished thit every church in the archdeaconry had its safe or strong chest, as also a book containing not only the minutes of the vestry Cr council meeting, but also an inventory of all the communion plate, and a liet of all deeds and papers be- longing to the church. In his recent charge to the clergy, the Bishep'gratef ally alluded to the liberality of their church in this diocese for the lest three years—a time of prolonged commercial depression. The amount raised for church, school, and mission-room building and enlargement, as well as for diocesan and parochial institutions and home and foreign missions, approached nearly a quarter of a million of money. Addressing, as he did, a great body of influential laymen, he might be forgiven if he drew attention to the fact that the clergy themselves participate to a very small extent in the results of this liberality. Thronghout the kingdom during the last 60 years no less a sum than 75 millione of money, it Was computed, had been contributed for ecclesiastical purposes; but with all this vast expendi- ture upon material structures they were threatened with the great peril of an impeverished clergy, and this danger is most pressing in the very poor and densely-popalated dis- tricts, where the claims upon the clergy for the support of various local objects are the seroneest. In this-diocese there are now 20 benefices under £2OO a year, and yet the amount contributed from the whole diocese for the aug- mentation of the poor benefices last year %VAS only £253. In many more cases the struggle he could testify was very severe, and there were, it was to be feared, clergy even in this diocese who had to drain to the dregs the bitter cup of poverty. It could not be easy to maintain the position of a Christian gen,leman on the income of an artisan. Almost every other church but their own had its eustentation fund to supple- ment the incomes of the poorer clergy. The Free Church of Scotland contributed in 1882 not less than £235,000 for this purpose. In their own church the need of such a fund is urgent—the question cmnot be long post- poned—the delay thus far has been discreditable ; its final disregard would be disaetrous. Meanwhile let him suggest that something might be done even in poor parishes. The weekly offertory was a soured and scriptural principle, and in no parishes more valuable than among the poor, whoa- cording to their limited means were within his experience the most liberal portion of their church community, and who would cheerfully take their part by frequent though small contributions in helping to make lighter many a heavy bur- den. And when this is not possible, or rather in all cases why should they not see that become the rule which is now the exception, namely, that the Easter offer- ings should be assigned to the clergy. At the risk of being misunderstood, he dare not hold his peace, and he would venture to press that a quiation once carlesely asked by a lady of fashion, and for which there was no waiting for a reply, " I wonder how the poorer clergy live ?"—shoald not be laid acids by them until they have found a satisfactory reply. They lived, he knew well, in stirring and stormy times, when even greater questions than these begin to agitate men's minds. Whether the establishment is worth maintaining—and whether Christianity itself can be defended—compered with such questions, his counsels were et slight importance. But they were practical, and if by their instrumentality during the ensuing year the services of their church should in any way have been amended and made more effective for their follow-men, and if the lives of the ministers themselves re- lieved from the darker shedows which from time to time fall acmes their ministrations of light and of life, they would have done much to justify the office to which they were that day to be admitted, wed would have accomplished that which will make their acceptance of it a happy memory in years to come.—The wardens then sabscribed the usual declarations, and were admitted to their offices.

LONGFORD DEPOT.

Sir,—lt is astonishing to me, an outsider, how the people who daily use the highway on the north side of Warrington, and live in the neighbourhood of that monntain of 111th— Longford depot—can quietly sit down and tolerate such a nuisance. I wonder, if this receptacle belonged to any private individual, how long your corporate officials would permit it to continue in such close proximity to a public highway. .13ut possibly their official nasal organs are not so sensitive as they otherwise would be if your Council was compelled to hold one meeting there weekly instead of in the luxurious rooms of your municipal palace.—l re- main, yours faithfully, PEDESTRIAN.

div.p: THE VIOAR OF KINGSLEY y. THE OWNERSII!P
OF GRAVES.

Sir,—The above subject has recently been brought before my notice, and has elicited a considerable amount of com- ment among the parishioners. As one of the latter, I wish to put the question before the readers of your impartial paper. The vicar has given his parishioners to understand that, providing they fail to erect a headstone within the space of six months after burial, they will forfeit all further I Claim to their relatives' graves mid this after they have had to pay for every inch of ground. Providing, too, he gets a stone he is compelled to consult the vicar as to its else and shape, for should he be so regardless of clerical authority as to forget to do so he will most likely have to pay double the fee, or have to take it back again. Now, sir, if this be not another instance of "clerical intolerance," fknow not what else to call it, and I for one say the sooner the better the Liberation Society has its way. Notwithstanding the dread that such an event is looked upon by the clergy, I am in- clined to think that they themselves through their actions will to a great extent be instrumental in bringing it to pass. —I beg, sir, to remain, yours respectfully, A PARISHIONER.

div.head: SPEAKMAN V. GRICE.
div.p: SPEAKMAN V. GRICE.

Sir,—The result of this case must have finally convinced the local Tories that they have been stranded and left be- hind by a progressive age. The time was, and that not as very long ago, when their political ancestors could incar- cerate wholesale those who said and did things they didn't like, but now a bumble scribe can flout them, as it were, in the very temple they have raised to the deities who pre- side over billiards and " nap," and get off " scot free." They have been taught a very useful ,lesson, but we owe Mr. Grice thanks for something more. fie has very oppor- tunely brought to light some of the ineradicable traits of the Tory character. The whole proceedings point the moral of the fable of the cat which was turned, through magical influences, into a fair damsel. The damsel for some time bore her" blashing honours "with unexceptionable pru- dence, and nobody who was ignorant of her origin would ever have thought she was anything else than what she seemed. But one day a little mouse ran across the floor, and then the old feline instincts re.asserted themselves, and, reverting to her origiital shape, she set upon the poor vic- tim with all the ancient ferocity. It is with the Tory party as it was with the oat in the fable. Tbe magic of an ex- tending franchise has compelled them to put on the fair semblance of liberality and tolerance, but let what seems to , he a favourable opportunity occur and they drop into their old methods as if still "to the manner born." The com- parison is not quite complete. When the oat fell back into its old condition it still had its former power, to do tele, chief ; but that is not so with the Tories. If you scratch a Tory you still ind a tyrant, but an impotent tyrant. There is the same willingness to wound, but there is not the same ability to strike. I think that is the lesson which may be derived from the whole aff air. ON-LOOKER.

div.head: IRISH NA.TIONAL•LSAGUE.
div.p: IRISH NA.TIONAL•LSAGUE.

Sir,—! am pleased that your correspondent "Clifford Dar," by his letter in your last Issue, has given me an op- portunity which, with your consent, I will embrace of mak- ing a few remarks concerning the Warrington branch of the above league. I have read with great attention this letter of a friend of tke Irish. and! gather that the strongest charge he brings against them is that in their 'resent movement of isolation they are making many mistakes. It may he so, but it is a matter of opinion, and! claim for the Irish elec- tors of Warrington, that they have a perfect right to adopt the me ins (providing they are constitutional) which in their opinion are beat calculated to advance the ease of their kith and kin at home, which they have adopted as their own cause. Many mistakes Irishmen have made in the past, and in my opinion they have made no slight one now when they considered they would be allowed to carry en peace- fully an indepeedent political organisation however con- stitutional or lawful it may be. Many of the Irishmen of Warringtm at the present time are under the impression, whether rightly or wrongly I know not, that certain mem- bers of the Liberal party are more opposed to their organisa- tion than any of the opposite party; and as the general election is close at hand, and neither Mr. Biggar nor any other into can at present say how the Irish vote will be mt. I would appeal to the prominent members ef the party, such as your correspondent appears to be, not by any act of theirs to foster such an opinion and thereby render it all the more difficult if the time should come for the Irishmen to cast in their lot again with the Liberal party. Your correspon- dent, of course, finds fault with Mr. Biggar for many things be sated, and for many others he left unsaid. I take this one as a sample; he is charged with having said that Pro- testant Ulster will in the future work for disunion along with the other three provinces. Now, Mr. Biggar never said anythiig of the kind, nor could such an interpretation be borpstly pat on his words.

He is also charged with not condemning the late outrages. Well, I don't understand why Irishmen should be called upon ou every occasion to denounce these outrages. Does any sensible Englishman believe that if the whole Parnel- lite °arty, in season and out of season, were to denounce these crimes that there would be one less committed ? I would as soon expect that Englishmen would believe that sioaultaneoue sermons from every bishop and clergymen and speeches from every Cabinet Minister in England denounc- ing theft would have the effect of stopping as much as one single pickpocket from cirrying on his nefarious practices. We as Irishmen know that the men who commit these out- rages are the greatest enemies of Ireland, and render the work G f Mr. Parnell and hie party all the more difficult of accomplishment.

I could net resist the temptation to nelice the terrible threat 1.1031 d Over the heads of Irishmen by your correspon- dent. If they dare to do that which they have a perfect right to do, viz, to vote according to the advice of Mr. Par- nell, Whigs and Tories are to make up their very few and trifling cliff4renct.s to puni.h the Irish electors. So that we 'shall be treatrd to the sublime spectacle at the next election of cur two worthy candidates, Mr. Crostield and Sir U. Green-all, heartily shaking hands and tossing up, I presume, as to who shall be the member for the borough. I only take ti-is as a good juke, and it must have been meant as such.

Now. sir, to the aid of those who take any prominent part in the locti branch of the National League, it is of the greatest moment that we should stand well with our Eng- lish fellow townsmen. I would ask them not to believe that we have all at once become incendiaries or advocates of baneful or dangerons doctrines, and therefore to be de- serving of nothing but coercion. R cher would I ask them to mike honest inquiries as to our rules and objects from those willing and anxious to answer, and to take past char- acers as some guarantee at least of present honesty of pur- pose. I have trespassed on your vilaible space more than I intended, but jest w:sh in conclusion to nwice your cur- respondent's tact sentence. He says " let Irishmen throw their meetings open.' I may say that such has been the case from the commencement, and we heartily invite any Englishmen who would care to be present at our meetings, and who would then see for themselves whether our organi- ! Cation was not honest, straight-forward and abovo botrd,— Yours, itc. CHAIRMAN.
